maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.

speechtext: In Committee on Private Bills:

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext:
I notice that .an unusually large number of divorce Bills are before the House this year. A few days ago a judgment was rendered by the Supreme Court of Manitoba, in which, if I mistake not, it was declared that henceforth the courts of Manitoba could grant divorces; that under the British North America Act, as amended when Manitoba came into Confederation, the English law was, in certain circumstances, to obtain in that province, and with it the application of the English law on the annulment of marriages. I believe that that pronouncement of the Supreme Court of Manitoba has mot been challenged. The same assertion was made, I believe, by the courts in one of the other western provinces.
iSir ROBERT BORDEN: I think it was decided in the same way in Saskatchewan, judging from a press report.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: I should like to have an expression of opinion from my right hon. friend with regard to this very important matter, because these decisions may alter completely our divorce proceedings in this Parliament. The opinion has been expressed in the other Chamber that larger powers should be conferred on the Senate with regard to the granting of divorces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext:
I know nothing of the decisions referred to except what has appeared in the public press. The Minister of Justice will doubtless be able to give some information on the subject after he has had opportunity of examining it. In four of the provinces, I believe- the Maritime Provinces and British Columbia-jurisdiction has hitherto been exercised by the courts in respect to the granting of divorces. So far as I know, jurisdiction in these provinces has never been

questioned. Similar jurisdiction is now asserted in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. It would be a very desirable consummation if these matters could be referred to the courts.
It is obvious to every one, who is familiar with divorce proceedings as conducted in the Senate, and in the courts, that the public interest is much better conserved by having such matters dealt with in a judicial way. In ,a divorce court it is the duty of the presiding judge, in an undefended case, to appoint a King's proctor, -who is charged with taking up the defence and of making such inquiry, by cross-examination of witnesses, and so forth, as to assure himself that there is no collusion between the parties. Whether or not any proceeding of that kind is taken before the Senate Committee, I do not know, but if so it is of recent years, because formerly no such practice prevailed. Apart from that; divorce is a proper subject for judicial inquiry if it is to be dealt with at all. I venture to express the hope that, if jurisdiction has been asserted by the courts in the three western provinces, it may transpire that their decision is well founded. It may also be proper for this House to consider whether by some means the jurisdiction could be transferred to the courts of the other provinces of Canada. At all event?, whenever the Senate is to consider a divorce Bill, the evidence upon which that Bill is founded, should be taken before a judicial tribunal and not by a committee of the Senate. Let us assume that there is some insuperable obstacle to vesting this jurisdiction in the courts of Ontario and Quebec. Would it not be better to have the inquiry conducted by a judge, the evidence heard by him, and the determination upon that evidence reported by him, leaving to the Senate the final adjudication by Act of Parliament? We can all, I think, agree that the present system is highly unsatisfactory.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext:
As I understand the question, it is not exactly as the Prime Minister puts it. Under the Act of Confederation, the Parliament of Canada alone has the power to legislate upon divorce. There is no doubt at all that, upon_ the broad terms of the constitution of this country, this Parliament has the right to establish a divorce court or to give jurisdiction. But this Parliament has always refrained from exercising that jurisdiction, and consequently, the' practice has grown up of parties seeking divorce, and who can not ob-
[Sif Robert Borden.]	-
tain it in their own province, coming to this Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: Just as used to be the case in Great Britain.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: Exactly, and that will be the case here until there is a divorce court established. The other question to which my right hon. friend referred is, as I understand it, that the province of Manitoba and also the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta claim they have_the right to establish divorce courts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: I understand the province of Manitoba claims its own courts have jurisdiction to decide divorce cases. If that is the situation, there is only one question at the present time. If any province which established its constitution at the time of Confederation has not the power to give its courts jurisdiction to grant divorces, have the new provinces now the power to give their courts jurisdiction to grant divorces? That is the question to-day, and it can, of course, be decided only by the supreme judicial authority, and the sooner there is a concrete case decided m regard to this point, the better it will be. If it be determined by the supreme judicial authority that the new provinces created since Confederation have the power to have divorces granted by their own courts, that wid simplify the question very much so far as the divorce business of this Parliament is concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: Would not my right hon. friend think it better to have those matters determined by ia judicial inquiry rather than by the Senate?

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext:
Here is a
province which asserts- that it has, under the constitution, the authority to have its own courts decide these matters. If that he so, the question of the interpretation of the constitution ought to be. determined before any other proceeding is taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: I do not think anybody contends that the province of Manitoba can create a divorce court. I think the contention is that the divorce court is already there, and there as a consequence of what this Parliament has done, whether it so intended or not.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext: Exactly.

maintopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL COURTS IN DIVORCE CASES.
speechtext:
As a layman, may I venture to give an expression- of opinion? Not only has Manitoba declared its power in the matter; it has done more,

it has exercised that power, (because it has recently 'granted a divorce, and I believe it is claimed that, under similar legislation, Saskatchewan and Alberta may do the same thing. I am one of those who have long felt it would be better if we could have one general divorce court for the' whole Dominion. I think we can all agree that the manner in which divorce cases are dealt with by this Parliament is not at all in accordance with, shall I say, moral conditions, nor in accordance with sound legislation. If we cannot have a general divorce court, might it not be a wise course for the Government to say that, wherever there is a divorce court clearly established in a province, the parties in that province shall go to that court? That would reduce the duties of this Parliament to the exercise of the functions of a divorce court only for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, until the good day shall come when even those provinces will be allowed to dispose of those matters in a better way.

THE YUKON ELECTION:

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.

speechtext: On the Order being called for the consideration of the second report of the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, covering the Yukon election.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. M. M. TWEEDTE (West Calgary):
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Although I was a member of the committee which dealt with the question of the Yukon election, and although that committee by a majority of one supported the motion of the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) I cannot concur in the report which the committee has presented to the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the hon. member to submit a motion?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes. The question which was really before the committee was in connection with the counting of the overseas vote for the Yukon constituency, in which Mr. F. T. Congdon and Dr. Alfred Thompson were the candidates. The general nomination day in the ridings throughout the Dominion of Canada in the last election was the nineteenth day of November, and polling day was on the seventeenth day of December. There was a deferred election in the Yukon, and under
the Act, December 31, 1917, was fixed as nomination day, and January 28, 1918, as polling day. After the election had been held in the Yukon, Mr. Congdon through his agents served notice of protest on the General Returning Officer at Ottawa, forbidding him to count the overseas vote, Mr. 'Congdon then having a majority of 110 on the home vote. The Returning Officer referred the matter to the Governor in Council, and an Order in Council was passed on the 26th February, and pursuant to that Order in Council, the record was submitted to the House for consideration. After the record had been submitted to the House the following motion Was passed:
That the special return of the General Returning Officer to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada concerning the election of a candidate to serve in the House of Commons for the Yukon Territory, he referred to the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections with power and authority to consider the same and the several documents therein alluded and to report their conclusion and their determination thereon to this House.
That limited the reference to the committee to the record >as submitted to the House, and there was no question of going beyond the limits of that reference and considering extraneous matter. So the question really before the committee was whether or not the overseas vote, which amounted to 256 for Thompson and 28 for Congdon, should be counted, thereby determining who should be entitled to sit for the Yukon. When the matter came before the Committee on Privileges and Elections it was thought desirable by all the members that both parties should have the privilege of appearing and consequently adjournments of the committee were had from time to time to give Mr. Congdon the opportunity of appearing and presenting fully his side of the case in connection with the election. It was generally understood, I believe, when these adjournments were made from time to time, that after Mr. Congdon had presented his case to the members of the committee, that committee itself would settle the question at issue. But, instead of arriving at a conclusion, as they were instructed to do by the order of this House, by a resolution which was adopted and reported to this House, and which reads as follows:
Resolved, that a stated case be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision.
-the committee shifts to an outside jurisdiction the responsibility which was placed upon it by this House.

Once having assumed the obligation of disposing of the Yukon case, it is my opinion that it should be disposed of by that committee, and that the matter should not be kept dragging along from time to time. If it is to be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, it simply means that the parties have to appear before some tribunal and state their case. They asked for an opportunity of stating their case before the Committee on Privileges and Elections and by frequent adjournments they were enabled to do that. After they have done that, it is my opinion that the committee should dispose of the matter one way or the other and report their findings on the question of fact to this House so that it may be finally disposed of.,
But, assuming, for the purposes of argument, that there may be ground upon which the contention of the mover of the resolution in the committee may be based, I submit that the resolution as it has been submitted to this House is impracticable 'because, if you will notice carefully the wording of the resolution, it says:
That a stated case be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision.
We will take the first words of the mover of that resolution, " a stated case." He is a good lawyer; he has had experience upon the bench of Nova Scotia, and he knows, as well as I know, what is meant by a stated case. It is the submission of a set of facts, or a set of questions, which must be agreed to by the parties themselves who are interested in these facts, for decision by a tribunal in the province in which the case *arises. When the hon. gentleman says "a stated case" he makes no suggestion as to who shall prepare such case and he makes no suggestion as to who shall be allowed to become parties to it. He takes out of their hands the rights to which they are entitled as a matter of ordinary statute law in any province of the Dominion. Does he suggest that the committee should state that case? Does he suggest that the members of the House of Commons should state that case? Does he suggest that the Governor in Council should state that case He makes absolutely no suggestion whatever in regard to the preparation of the stated case, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is beyond the power of this House to prepare any stated case for any court or for any judges in the Dominion.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I did suggest-

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary to tell' me to sit down. I wish to remind my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) that I suggested in the committee that a subcommittee of the committee should prepare a stated case. Perhaps it escaped the ear of my hon. friend, but that is what I suggested.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There was a resolution directing that the evidence be printed and submitted to this House, and I submit that we are bound by the record as it appears here and by the resolution as it appears in the Votes and Proceedings. Then, we come to the second question. He says that a "stated case shall be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision." My language on that point, if I cared to make it so, might perhaps be stronger than the occasion warrants. But think of a member of the House of Commons, in his place, moving that this question shall be submitted first to the Supreme Court of the Dominion of Canada, a body in which we are supposed to have the most eminent jurists in this country, or, in the alternative, to two judges of the province of Ontario. He practically says: "I would just as soon have the judgment of two judges of the province Of Ontario on this question as the judgment of the whole Supreme Court of Canada." We must feel that this is more or less of an insult to the Supreme Court of this country to put it in contrast with two judges of the province of Ontario. Passing from the judges of the Supreme Court and the two judges of the province of Ontario, what justification is there for presenting to this House any resolution which would remove the consideration of this important question from the jurisdiction in which the question arises, namely, the jurisdiction of the Yukon Territory? Are these men to be brought from the Yukon Territory down to Ottawa, or Toronto, when it is purely a Yukon matter, and when, under the 'Controverted Elections Act, the 'Supreme Court of the Yukon Territory has jurisdiction? If the hon. gentleman wishes to be absolutely fair, and to be bound by the principles of law in regard to 'this question, I submit to the members of this House that there is absolutely no justification [DOT] whatever for removing either one of the parties from the

jurisdiction of the court in which the question (before the House arises.
I think that this is a matter which should be disposed of by a committee of this House. I further think that if it is not so disposed of there is no authority whereby the members of this House can submit this case to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges in Ontario. If they do, it spems to me that they must stretch the Supreme Court Act to an extent which was never contemplated by the framers of that Act. If they could possibly get it in under section 60 it would have to come in under subsection (b) of the Supreme Court Act, which reads i
Important questions of law or fact touching:-[DOT]
(b)	the constitutionality or interpretation of any Dominion or provincial legislation
It seems to me that we are not concerned in this case with any important question of law or fact touching the constitutionality or interpretation of the statutes under which elections are held. I submit that under the Act the principle upon which soldiers shall cast their vote is clearly laid down. I .submit that the time in which that vote must be cast is clearly stated in the Military Voters' Act and that there is no 'question of constitutionality and no question of interpretation. We must take that Act and read it as we find it and if we do not, then we must (be men enough to say whether or not the votes of these men overseas are going to he counted either for Dr. Thompson or foT Mr. F. T. Congdon.
For these Teasons I am going to ask this House to refer' the matter back to the committee, and I ask that in accordance with the principle which is laid down in the 3rd edition of Bourinot's Parliamentary Practice, at page 556, and which reads:
A report may be referred back to a committee for further consideration, or with instructions giving them power to amend the same in any respect. In this way a committee may regularly reconsider and even reverse a decision it has previously arrived at.
If my hon. friends have concluded that they have arrived-at a decision, which |Oon-clusion I do not concur in, the matter still should be referred back to' the committee, who have absolute power to deal with it in any manner they see fit. Therefore, for the purpose of bringing this matter to an issue I would move:
That the second report of the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections be not concurred in, hut that it be referred back to the said Committee for further consideration and to report thereon.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I want
to present the case to the House, not in
any legal way at all, but simply for the purpose of appealing to the sense of justice of hon. members, and also to their sense of fairness. Let me begin by stating that if there was delay in the consideration of this case by the Committee on Privileges and Elections, it was not due to any fault on the part of either of the parties concerned, nor was it due to any fault on the part of the members of the committee. My hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie), should not complain of this, because at the meeting of the committee which took place on Tuesday, April 21, according to the printed report of the proceedings of the committee, he first of all moved a motion and then withdrew it. Here is what the hon. gentleman said:
I will withdraw the motion I made and substitute the following:
That this Committee adjourn until eleven o'clock, on Thursday, May 2nd, and if at that time Mr. Congdon has not left the city of Vancouver for Ottawa, then this Committee should proceed to dispose of the case in his absence.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In his absence?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes.
If he has left then we will have a reasonable adjournment to allow him to get to the city of Ottawa.
That motion was carried.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I would like to make an explanation. I made no complaint whatever. I think the committee only acted fairly in adjourning from time to time to allow the interested parties to appear before them.	'

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Against the wishes of the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I moved the resolution.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am saying this in fairness to the hon. member. I am not complaining, of his attitude at all, I simply want to show that the committee used all diligence in proceeding. Again on May 2, Mr. Tweedie moved:
That the Committee adjourn until Tu'esday morning next at ten-thirty o'clock, and then proceed to the consideration of the matter referred to.
That motion also was carried. That brought us up to the meeting of Tuesday, May 7, when Mr. Congdon was present, and the case was proceeded with. I mention this en passant, Mr. Speaker, in order to show that there was no fault to be found on account of the delays occasioned in the

consideration of this case. The proceedings went on equitably and with all due haste. The consideration of the Yukon election was taken in different phases, and I am not going to review those phases. I merely want to point out that both candidates seemed to agree upon one thing: That the nomination papers were not to be held for any further consideration by the committee, but that they were to be accepted, the whole case then being reduced to a point of law as to whether the votes cast by the soldiers overseas should be considered in the election or not. Those members of the committee who are now present will, I think, bear me out in that statement. Nominations for the Yukon took place on December 31, 1917, and the polling day was fixed for January 28, 1918. It was contended by Mr. Congdon that any votes that were given before the day of nomination should not be counted in the election, and he supported his contention by citing different sections of the Elections Act, and notably of the Military Voters' Election Act, laying stress particularly upon section 6, and subsection 1 of section 8, the section reading:
That at the expiration of the time'for nominating the candidatesthat is to say at the expiration of the 31st of December. 1917. And then section 8:
Polls shall he held in such camps or other places in Canada or elsewhere, as shall be assigned to the charge of presiding officers for the purposes of this part. Those held without Canada shall be maintained open during such sufficient number of days and during such hours as military exigencies will permit, but so that no polling shall commence before the day following that of the nomination of candidates, nor continue after eight o'clock of the evening of the day for holding the poll within Canada.
Let me again read the last words of the section just quoted:
but so that no polling shall commence before the day following that of the nomination of candidates?
The nomination of candidates, I repeat, was on December 31st, 1917, and according to the Military Voters' Act, no polling of the soldiers could take place before the day following that of the nomination of candidates. There are certain exceptions to this, and notably in the case of emergencies. Subsection 5 of the said clause 8 reads:
In any ease where, for any reason, unless the vote of a military elector is immediately taken it is likely that he may not subsequently be able to vote, the Deputy Presiding Officer may take such vote otherwise than at a formally held poll, but such vote shall be so taken

in the presence of the Deputy Scrutineers, or failing either or both, of a military elector, or .two military electors, who shall, together with the Deputy Presiding Officer, sign upon the envelope in which the ballot is inserted a certificate that the vote was taken under this subsection, and the reasons which made it necessary.
In the opinion of the majority of the members of the Committee, the whole question then resolved itself into this simple legal question: Are the votes cast prior to nomination day for the Yukon, to be considered as votes cast in that election? In order to do justice to born candidates, the majority of the committee decided that, as it was purely a legal question, the matter should be referred in a stated case to the Supreme Court oif Canada for decision, My hon. friend from North Cape Breton {Mr. McKenzie) moved that a subcommittee should draft the stated case to be presented to the Supreme Court. I do not wish to enter more fully into this question; I simply desire to. submit the matter to the House in fairness and justice to the people of Canada who are concerned in the election of a candidate to represent one of the constituencies of this Dominion, and in justice also to the two candidates themselves. Neither the one nor the other has any advantage to gain by referring the matter to the Supreme Court; neither the one nor the other is under any disadvantage through the fact that the Supreme Court, being a judicial body, accustomed to decide questions of law, will decide the one question that was up before the committee as to whether the votes cast before nomination day in the Yukon Territory should be considered or not. And for that purpose, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move in amendment to the motion of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie), seconded by the hon. member for North Cape Breton:
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
That this House concurs in the said resolution of the Committee on Privileges and Elections presented to the House on the 13th day of May, concerning the election of a candidate to serve in the House of Commons for the Yukon Territory; that a stated case be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I have not had opportunity to consider whether the amendment is of the nature of a negative motion. I reserve the right to determine subsequently whether it is in order or not.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I shall be very brief in second-

ing the amendment of the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin). Perhaps I might, in the first instance, answer briefly the mover of the motion (Mr. Tweedie). He suggested that I had no business to -move that this pure question of law should be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, and particularly that I had no right to say that, it dt did not go to the Supreme Court of Canada it should go to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario. I do not know what the hon. member means by saying that I was trying to draw an insulting comparison between the Supreme Court of Canada and two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario. Nothing could be further from my mind than to suggest such thing. The Supreme Court of Canada is par excellence the court to which any question of law which this Parliament wants decided should go. There is no question about that. I am asked why I suggested two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario. The reason is that ordinarily any person who complains about an election has a right to petition, and by this petition he gets the benefit of the decision of two judges of the Supreme Court of a province. If he belongs to Ontario, or if the case is to be tried in the province of Ontario, he gets the benefit of the judicial knowledge of two judges of the Supreme Court of that province. That is why it seemed to me that if it was thought best to proceed along the line of a petition, it should go to the Supreme Court of the nearest and most convenient province. I did say in Committee that I was perfectly satisfied that it should go to the Yukon if they had judges there competent to deal with it, but that I thought it would be more convenient to submit the facts and argue the case before judges in Ottawa or Toronto, or some place close at hand, than to send men out to the Yukon to argue the case. That is the reason I suggested that the case should go forward to such a court as would be capable of dealing with it if it were proceeded with as a petition.
The submission by Parliament of questions of law to judges is not a new practice. It is an old practice in England, where the House of Commons and the House of Lords for many years have been in the habit of drafting questions of law difficult for them to decide and sending them down to judges of High Courts in England. The same practice is in vogue here. And where there is a question that is purely one of law, I submit to every sensible man in this House that the place to decide that question of law is a court properly constituted for that purpose. I have every respect, Sir, for the judgment and decision and conscientious beliefs and scruples of every man in this House. But we are in a House divided into two camps politically; we are a partisan body; we cannot escape from it. There may be a few here who are not partisans, but taking the House as a whole, it is a partisan body, and I am sure, Sir, that you and any reasonable man in this House will agree that a partisan body is not the proper court or -institution to which to submit the deciding of a cold-blooded proposition of what the law is upon any given point. I felt that the same ideas and the same condition of things existed in the committee to which this matter was submitted, and I moved, therefore, on that occasion that it be taken out of the realm of party politics and sent where there would be no politics, and where the question of law would be dealt with purely and simply as the highest court in the land can deal with it.
The hon. member for Calgary seemed to express a doubt as to whether-we have jurisdiction to send this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada. Of course, the House, as such, may not do so, although I think it is easily within the inference. But Section 60 of the Supreme Court Act, Chapter 139 of the Revised Statutes of Canada deals with questions of this kind. There are several things that we can submit to the Supreme Court of Canada. One is:
The interpretation of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1886.
Another is:
The constitutionality or interpretation of any Dominion or provincial legislation.
Even if the section went no further than this, we could very well send this matter to the Supreme Court for decision. But it proceeds:
(c)	the appellate jurisdiction as to educational matters, hy The British North America Act, 1S67, or by any other Act or law vested in the Governor in Council; or,
(d)	the powers of the Parliament of Canada, or of the legislatures of the provinces, or of the respective Governments thereof, whether or not the particular power in question has been or is proposed to be executed.
If under these provisions of the law any doubt exists as to our power to refer this matter to the Supreme Court, surely the following subsection is sufficiently sweeping:
(e)	any other matter, whether or not in the opinion of the court ejusdem generis with the foregoing enumerations, with -reference to which the Governor in Council sees fit to submit any such question.

Under this provision the Governor in Council has wide power to submit to the Supreme court any question which should properly be decided by that body. I think that I have made it clear, therefore, that the Governor in Council has power and authority to submit this particular question to the Supreme Court. In any case, it should be submitted to some court satisfactory to the House and to the Governor in Council. I simply want to have a judi

cial finding upon a matter which is purely a question of law. The Prime Minister said this morning that in divorce cases it was unsatisfactory that questions of fact should be determined by the Senate or by any political body. If it is undesirable to try questions of fact or of law before a political body such as the Senate or this House,	it	is equally	undesirableto try	a	question of	this- kind.
While we have no power to send divorce cases to the Supreme Court of Canada, we we have power to refer to them a political question of this kind. When we did have jurisdiction to deal with thesei political questions-perhaps we have it yet-that jurisdiction was not vested in such a committee as we had the other day. As early as 1873 the then great leader of the Conservative party, Sir John A. Macdonald, as may be seen by reference to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, introduced an Act into the House taking the jurisdiction in this matter entirely out of the realm of polities and placing it in the hands of the judges. Since I became a member of this House I have heard no hint of any such thing as an election trial before this House. If any such trials -have taken place since 1873, I am not familiar with them. The feeling has been that the House should not try questions of law such as arise in election cases, but refer them to a competent court for decision.
Some hon. gentlemen may say that the case is plain; why should it not be decided on the spot? My answer is this: if this *were a simple proposition, the Governor in Council, a body composed of very excellent lawyers, would at once direct the general returning officer to decide the case without delay. But they deemed the question of sufficient importance to cause them to issue an injunction to the general returning officer, instructing him not to decide the question. Mr. O'Connor, the general returning officer, is a good lawyer who has had a good deal of experience at the bar of Nova Scotia and has dealt with many fMr. McKenzie.]
intricate cases. He is well known to some of the members of Council, particularly to the Prime Minister. But it was deemed advisable to estop that gentleman from deciding this point, and to send it here to be dealt with. It is a pity that at the very outset this case was not sent to the court instead of this House. But if an error was made in sending it here, we have not yet gone too far; we should take the earliest opportunity of sending it to a proper court for decision. The member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) made a remark the other night-page 1815 of Hansard-which emphasizes what I mean when I say that this is not a proper court to try such cases. He said:
I would form my opinion to some extent on the past history of the applioant, his or lier experience, and the work that he or she had done, and the efficiency displayed in the particular branch in which the party had been engaged. If I were to undertake to give an opinion on a lawsuit, for instance, as to the grounds for submitting a case to the Court of Appeal, I would probably make a fool of myself.	.
That is what one of the brightest men in this House said about departing from his own sphere and passing judgment on something which his experience and training did not qualify him to decide. We should all be pleased that there is a court to which we can with confidence appeal concerning this point of law. Both sides will have full opportunity of arguing the matter. If the Supreme Court of Canada or two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario decide that although one or other of these gentlemen was not nominated when the votes were cast, nevertheless the ballots should be counted one way or the other, then the person in whose favour that decision is given may be declared elected by the returning officer, and that will be an end to the whole business. No matter how we decide the point in this House, the decision will be looked upon with ridicule as a partisan one. The proper, the logical, the fair thing for this House to do is to refer to the Supreme Court the record, without change, as it has been handed down by the general returning officer, Mr. O'Connor. Then the decision will be regarded by all as satisfactory ; the procedure will be fair and constitutional, and a precedent will be established which may safely be followed in future. I have much pleasure in seconding the amendment.

iblooded question of law and nothing else. There is a question of law involved, it is true; part of the question is a question of law. I shall see if I can define to the iHouse this fine, hair-splitting question of law.

speechtext:
The question is as to whether or not the term "nomination" day in the Military Voters' Act means the nomination day in each of the several constituencies, or means the general nomination day of Canada; whether or not the intention of Parliament was that the voters overseas should toe all voted together in their respective constituencies- at the same time over the same month, or whether they should (be parted into camps and: some voted in one period in one election and some in another, depending altogether when the vote should take place in the constituency in which they exercise their franchise. I was present when the Military Voters' Act was before this House; many other hon. members also- were here, and I would like hon. gentlemen to search the records of Hansard and ascertain wherever -a dioutot arose in the fertile brains of any member of this House as to whether or not the vote o-f the soldiers overseas was all to be taken, at the same time. Nobody ever questioned the thing; but it is contended- I shall not say rightly or wrqngly, although I have an opinion-that according to the strict interpretation of the rules of law, *the law is, that unless the overseas votes -of a special constituency, namely the Yukon constituency, were taken after the day of nomination in that constituency, which day was the 29th of- December, long after the whole general votes were taken overseas, then tho-se votes could not be counted at all. It is argued, in support of that, that, inasmuch as they were taken previously, commencing on the day of the general nomination, the 19th of November, those overseas voters had voted without a full knowledge, -a-t all events without official knowledge, of the candidates for whom they were voting. When I say that, I think I have said, in favour of the merits of contention, everything which has a right to consideration. That is a question of law; that may be called a cold-blooded question of law, and if there ever was something cold-blooded, in the nature of the legal interpretation, I think it is that.
But there i-s more than -that involved; there is involved the question of right and

justice; there is the question of the intent of Parliament, whatever be the specific interpretation of ,the law. There is the question of what, if that is the law, it is the duty of this Parliament to do in relation to the votes so cast. Was that duty not committed -to the committee? If it should be found, On a cold-blooded question of law, that the correct interpretation w-as that these votes must be all disregarded, was it not the duty of the committee to determine whether or not Parliament should allow that evidence to go forward and deny the franchise to one-fifth of the electorate of that constituency, o-r whether it was the duty of this House -to give to these men the franchise that it was within their power to exercise?
It has been argued on the part of some, as I stated before, that these men did not know officially who the candidates were, and that may be -quite correct. It is argued cu the part of others that these men knew vho the Government was, and who the Opposition was, and knew what the issue cf the election was, and to the utmost of the power reposed in them, under the law of Canada, exercised the franchise which was given to them; and if it should be found, in the determination of the law alone, that because they voted before the twenty-ninth day of December their votes should1 not be counted, then we would have to decide whether that was sufficient reason for the Parliament of Canada to say to them: "Because you voted without knowing who the candidates were we will legalize the franchise you exercised1 so far as it was in your power to exercise it." They voted for the Government or for the Opposition; they voted for or against the issue of conscription; they exercised the franchise to the full extent it was in their power to exercise it when they cast their ballot, and if we decide that having done so there is a legal objection to counting the votes, then what is the duty of Parliament in the premises? Is it the duty of Parliament to legalize those votes, or shall we say that on account of the fault of Parliament these men shall remain disfranchised throughout the life of this Parliament? That was the question submitted for determination to the Privileges and Election Committee by a resolution of this House. The Privileges and Elections Committee have made no report on that question at all, but on the motion of an hon. member of -the committee it was decided without discussion, and I blame no one for that, simply to refer the coldblooded question of law to the Supreme

207i5
Court of Canada or to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario.
Now in the first place the only way to submit a stated case, as was very clearly explained by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedde), is for all the parties interested in that case to agree upon a wording, and then lay the case before the tribunal for determination. Who are all the parties interested in this case? Are they only the late hon. member for the Yukon, Mr. Thompson, and Mr. Congdon, the Opposition candidate. Is nobody else interested? Are the people of the territory itself not interested, irrespective entirely of the personal rights of these m.en? Are the voters overseas, some 325 men, not interested, entirely irrespective of the rights of Mr. Congdon and Mr. Thompson? Are they not to be represented in making a stated case to the Supreme Court or to two judges Of the Supreme Court of Ontario? And if they are to be represented, how are they to be represented, and who is to decide that matter? None of these questions are dealt with in this Teport. Furthermore, I contend that even if this House had adopted the report and went further, and did what the committee refused to do laid out the machinery by which this stated case would be prepared, and had the matter submitted to the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court would be compelled to decide they had no jurisdiction to try the case at all. From no other source can the Supreme Court have jurisdiction except from the common law of Canada and the statute law, and I argue that neither common law nor statute law gives the Supreme Court any jurisdiction to hear and determine a report from a committee of Parliament.
I do not think any elaboration of my own opinion would be very convincing to the House on a matter of this nature, but I take the liberty of quoting the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice on this point, which is to the effect that neither the Supreme Court of Canada nor any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario would have power to hear and determine such a matter, merely upon its submission by this House, as the report of the Privileges and Elections Committee. The opinion is contained in a memorandum to the Prime Minister dated May 15 and is as follows:
The Select Standing Committee of the Houses of Commons on Privileges and Elections, upon reference of the special return of the General Returning Officer to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery concerning the Yukon election, recom-
131i	I !*;	'
mends that a stated case be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision.
Obviously such a reference may be made only if it be within the jurisdiction of the court or the judges, either inherently or by statute, to determine upon such a reference the question submitted by the stated case. Now there can be no doubt til'it it is not at common law a part of the duty of the courts, or the judges, to determine questions referred by a committee of the House of Commons.
It is provided by the Supreme Court Act, section 61 that the court, or any two judges thereof shall examine and report upon any private Bill or petition for a private Bill presented to the Senate or House of Commons, and referred to the court under any rules or orders made by the Senate or House of Commons.
This section describes a jurisdiction somewhat analogous to that which the House of Lords exercises to put questions of law to the judges, the answer to which may be necessary to the House in its legislative capacity. The House of Lords also in its judicial capacity may consult the judges, but that power is exercised only for the purpose of obtaining advice with respect to the disposition of pending cases, and as to this the jurisdiction is different from any which is possessed by either House of Parliament in Canada. With respect to advice upon legislative questions the judges in England, as the cases show, have been very careful to confine their answers to the strict legal construction of existing statutes, and they have asked to be excused from answering questions which go beyond this. It will be perceived, however, that section 61 of the Supreme Court Act falls far short of enabling a committee of the House of Commons to submit a stated case with regard to an election return, and, except for section 61, there is no legislation authorizing the court or the judges to advise the House, or any committee. The business of the court is to determine questions raised between parties impleaded in judicial proceedings, and moreover no doubt to execute any judicial duty which may he imposed by statute but as the proceeding recommended by the committee is entirely novel and not within any jurisdiction which the court possesses, it is out of question that the court would decline to adjudicate upon any case submitted by the committee, or by the House upon the recommendation of the committee, and I apprehend that the only way m wnirh the committee's recommendation could he made effective would he by statute imnosing a new duty upon the court.
Words could not be clearer as to the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice on the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear such a commitment did this Parliament adopt the report. So upon the score of that the court suggested would have no jurisdiction whatever to determine the issue if it were committed to it, on the score, secondly, that there is no method of putting the case to the court if they had jurisdiction, and on the score, thirdly, and most strongly of all, that it is the duty of a committee of this House to discharge an obligation imposed upon them by this

House and not to seek to evade that charge, and because this House is bound in justice to itself not to evade its duty until it has exhausted all its powers under a committee, I think we ought to adopt the motion of the hon. member for Calgary and refer the matter back.

speechtext:
I do not think the matter raised by the hon. member should affect the case now before Parliament, but on that matter there are very conflicting opinions
Hon. W. iS. FIELDING: Mr. Speaker, if we were dealing with the merits of this question we might bring it home to ourselves, in one of our nearby constituencies, without going to the far-away Yukon. Suppose that on the 19th November in any constituency in Canada the nominations were being made and somebody should come up and say: " Look here, Mr. Returning Officer, we thought this election was going on some time ago; we held a meeting in our district, we have been doing some voting and we propose that you shall count the votes given some weeks ago when there were no candidates in the field." What would the returning officer say? Surely he would say at once : " There is no candidate in the field until the candidate is nominated, and when there is no candidate in the field, votes can hardly be counted in an election which comes on later." That seems to me to be reason and common sense. But we are not called upon in any degree to go into the merits of this question here because it seems to he rather a legal question. I was somewhat surprised) at the argument put up by the Hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) when he said the committee had no discretion in this matter. . We passed a resolution in this House referring the matter to a committee. I think I am justified in saying that in so doing we expressed no opinion at all. We simply referred this matter to the committee for inquiry and investigation. " No," says the Minister of the Interior, " we did not; we referred it to you with a command to

settle this question yourselves." Surely that cannot have been the spirit in which this House adopted the reference. Surely it was referred to the committee with the understanding that they should deal with it as they thought best. But even if there were that command given, even if they were instructed to inquire and come to a determination and if, in their judgment they should come to the conclusion that the matter was one which might properly be referred to the court, would they not be justified in reporting accordingly? Would my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior seriously claim that because of the words of the reference, because of the instructions that they were to inquire into the matter, and to reach a conclusion and report, they were thereby not permitted to make a report advising a reference to the court? 'The essence of this question, as between the two motions, seems to be this: The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) desires that the matter shall be .settled by the House and by a committee ot the House. He says that he desires to refer this matter back to the committee in order that the committee of the House may settle it at once. In other words, he does not want any legal reference at all. On the other hand, the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) has proposed that this matter be referred to the higher courts. The essence of the question is whether this House desires to settle this .thing itself or whether it desires to obtain a judicial opinion on a judicial matter. That seems to me to be the essence of the whole question. If the machinery .whereby that judicial tribunal is to be created is dieifective, by all means let us try to make it effective. The essence of . the whole question is: " Shall we deal with this matter in the House or by a judicial reference?" On that question I do not believe there should be any hesitation in the mind of any reasonable man. Parliament has a long history in Tegard to the question of the trial of controverted elections. Away hack in the early times of the House of Commons of Great Britain from which we draw our inspiration and practice it was found inconvenient for the House to deal with these matters because many difficulties arose from that practice, and more than that, they obtained a distinctly partisan decision. And so, in the progress of time the procedure was changed and it was agreed that a committee should be chosen to deal with these matters. For some years the committee procedure was followed. But there again they found that they were using

partisan machinery to deal with questions which were not properly the subject of partisan consideration, After further years of progress it was decided that the committee system was wrong. I have a recollection of such cases' in our provincial legislature. One arose in Nova Scotia in my boyhood days long before Confederation, as a result of which party feeling and great personal bitterness existed for a long period afterwards. The case was tried by a committee of the House and a decision was reported favourable to one candidate and confirming in his seat the member who had been returned. I remember that a very distinguished statesman, who afterwards rose to great eminence in this House, when, in fater years another distinguished man was proposed to be made chief justice of Nova Scotia, declared in the political journal which he controlled that the latter was unfit-to be a judge in Nova Scotia because he had perjured himself in that election case. That is the kind of thing you get if you proceed to deal with these matters through a party tribunal in the form of a committee of the House. There have been some cases even in this Parliament in which it was felt that that procedure was very unsatisfactory and by the common consent of all parties this Parliament resolved that it was incompetent (to discuss questions of that character and that in fairness and justice all such matters should be referred to a judicial tribunal under the Controverted Elections Act.

CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I say that Parliament
decided it would no longer have the committee system and that there should he created a judicial tribunal for the performance of such duties. But Parliament has not absolutely dispossessed itself of authority in such matters. There are cases in which Parliament will still take action, but they are not cases which are purely matters of dispute between the parties. Take the ease in which an Irish constituency returned O'Donovan Rossa. It was reported to Parliament that he was a convict. He was known to be a convict, and not only a convict but actually in prison. There arose
a question as to whether he should he debarred from taking his seat. It was argued that he was not qualified to take his seat, and Parliament decided that it would not allow him to take his seat. There was no dispute as to the validity of the return; it was a question of qualification or disqualification, and it was therefore a question with which Parliament itself should deal. John Mitchell was returned by acclamation for Tipperary. John Mitchell was an escaped political convict, and Parliament decided that he was disqualified. There was no dispute as to the return, but Parliament determined that he was not qualified and it ordered a- new writ to issue. John Mitchell became a candidate again mation, and I would ask hon, members to observe the distinction which Parliament made. John Mitchell having been elected by acclamation, there was no question as to the procedure (by the returning officer; it was purely a question of qualification, and the House of Commons decided that it should have the say as to that. But when John Mitchell became a candidatae again he was opposed, and the question became more than one of qualification; it became a question of dispute between two' candidates. Then Parliament said: "It is not a matter within our power; that must go to a judicial tribunal."
Some years ago a very famous case occurred in this House, commonly known as the King-Baird case.	It will be admitted by anybody who reads the evidence that a/11 the facts in that case were in favour of Mr. King. But Mr. Baird had been declared returned by the returning officer. The issue was threshed out, and, it became more or less a matter of party -controversy. However, the conclusion reached was that Parliament ought not to take any action. Sir John Thompson, who was then Minister of Jus' tice, made a very strong argument based simply on the ground that it was a judicial matter in which Parliament should not interfere. Now the equities were so strongly with Mr. King that public opinion forced Mr. Baird, although he was sustained in his seat, to resign' and be again elected. But notwithstanding that the case, in point of equity, was so strongly in favour of Mr. King, Sir John Thompson took the ground: this is not a question for Parliament, hut one for the judicial tribunals of the country. I do not think this should be a matter of party controversy. We are going to make precedents in this matter to-day, and hon. gentlemen on both sides should be

chary of creating precedents that may be embarrassing in the future. If there is one thing more than another which has been clearly understood' it is that the House of . Commons of Canada ought not of itself to undertake to deal with questions of this kind, because of the danger of partisan-snip entering into the matter, and, therefore, Parliament would be acting wisely in determining upon a reference to the judiciary of the country. If the machinery by which that can be done .is not effective, let us improve it, but let us not try to settle the matter here in violation of the long traditions of Parliament, which declare that the courts, and not the House of Commons, are the proper authorities to decide matters of this kind.
