speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is certainly indebted to the hon, member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) for having put this matter before it in its proper light. As he rightly said, the report of the Committee on Privileges and Elections was certainly not a refusal on the part of the members of that committee to deal with the question referred to them by the order of reference of this House. The order of reference reads:
That the Special Return of the General Returning Officer to the 'Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada concerning the election of a candidate to serve in the House of Commons for the Yukon Territory be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections with power and authority to consider the same and the several documents therein alluded to and to report their conclusion and determination thereon to this House.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to t'he contrary notwithstanding, the Committee on Privileges and Elections have considered the matter referred to them, a.nd they have reported their conclusion and determination, to the House. After having heard the arguments of both parties, they have determined that the question resolves itself into a mere question of law, and that it should net be left to the members of the committee, which may be a partisan committee, to decide, but that it should be decided by judicial authority. That is the gist of the ease. I am not concerned as to whether the drafting is defective; that may easily be remedied by the House. Even, if an Act of Parliament is necessary to give effect to the views of the Committee on

Privileges and Elections, such an Act may very expeditiously be passed.
The question as to who is to represent a particular constituency in the Canadian House of Commons is of very great importance. It is just as important a question as whether a county'will be represented at all, and interests not only the people of the particular constituency affected, but the people of the country as a whole. All citizens of Canada are interested in the ability, integrity, qualifications and standing of all and any of the members of the House of Commons. So the question of considering the conflicting claims of two gentlemen who assert their right to a seat in this House must be dealt with without any party spirit and free from all political bias on the part of the members of this House. By the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, this Parliament, following the precedent of the British Parliament, has left to judicial authority the decision of all questions relating to controverted elections. The principle goes to the extent, as is asserted by British constitutional authority, that the only question which Parliament has reserved to itself to deal with is the question as to whether a proper or fit person has been returned in obedience to the writ. I will quote the words of the late Sir John Thompson, then Minister of Justice, uttered in the House of Commons in 1887, as found on page 157 of Hansard of that year.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him if he does not consider that the whole question is comprised in the disenfranchisement or otherwise of the soldiers?

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I will deal with
that later on. Here are the words of the late Sir John Thompson:
Since the change which I have referred to, and by which Parliament has renounced its rights to deal with the matter of controverted elections, there has been fully recognized in the various discussions that have taken place in the Imperial House of Commons, this principle, that everything has been transferred to the judiciary in connection with controverted elections, excepting the one question of the disqualification of persons who have been returned to Parliament. As was said by Sir Henry James, in 1882, in the oase of Michael Davitt, the only question which Parliament has reserved to itself to deal with is the question whether a proper person has been returned in obedience to the writ As was explained by Lord Coleridge and Lord Selborne in a previous debate in 1870, that reservation is not in conflict with the Statute which says that the election shall only be contested by an election petition, because the House has to consider whether the writ has been obeyed which com-

rnanded the electors of the shire, or the county, to return a suitable person to sit in that House. The House, therefore, is still seized of the right to decide whether the writ has been obeyed by the election of a person who is tit and proper to sit in that House. But as soon as the question has been decided as to the qualification of the person so returned, the conduct of the returning officer, or the number of votes which were received, the conduct of the candidates, and every other question connected with the election, or with the conduct of the returning officer, has been relegated to the judiciary, and the House has always declined to exercise its functions and its power to interfere.
I shall also quote the words of May in his "Parliamentary Practice:"
Before the year 1770, controverted elections were tried and determined by the whole House of Commons, as mere party questions, upon which the strength of contending factions might be tested.
In order to prevent so notorious a perversion of justice, the House consented to submit the exercise of its privilege to a tribunal constituted by law, which, though composed of its own members, should be appointed so as to secure impartiality, and the administration of justice according to the laws of the land, and under the sanction of oaths.	*
Further on he says:
This principle was maintained, with partial alterations of the means by which it was carried out, until 1868, when the jurisdiction of the House, in the trial of controverted elections was transferred by statute to the courts of law.
In this country this principle has been accepted in our Dominion Controverted Elections Act. Section 91 of that Act says:
All elections shall he subject to the provisions of this Act, and shall not be questioned otherwise than in accordance herewith.
And this applies, Mr. Speaker, even when no return has been made. Section 11 of the Act says:
The petition presented under this Act may he in any prescribed form; hut, if or in so far as no form is prescribed, it need not he in any particular form, but it must complain of the undue election or return of a member or that no return has been made, or that a double return has been made, or of matter contained in any special return made,
And so on. And Section 8 says:
Whenever a petition under this Act, complaining of no return, is presented, such order may be made thereon by the court as is deemed expedient for compelling a return to he made.
So Ithat the matter of controverted elections is entirely left to judicial authority, - whether a return has been made by the returning officer, or whether no return at all has been made.
Of all cases, Sir, it seems to me that the present instance should he decided according to that principle. There are no questions of fact discussed or even challenged. The Act of 1917 amending the election law must <be interpreted according to the views of Dr. Thompson, or it must be interpreted according to those of Mr. Congdon. This Parliament cannot make a law for the purpose of changing a law which was passed last year in order that the change can be made applicable to an election which has actually taken place. Retroactivity in a case of that kind would be immoral on its very face. So the law as iit is must be interpreted, and what the members of this House must ask themselves is: What is the proper authority to interpret that law?
I respectfully submit that the judicial authority, not this Parliament, is the only [DOT] proper authority to interpret the statute passed last year. Let me ask members of the House this simple question: Do they consider that they are as well qualified as the members of the Supreme Court of Canada to interpret a law or to decide a case arising from the interpretation of a law, either from the point of view of legal knowledge, of judicial experience or even of impartiality? For my part, I admit that my qualification for that duty is not equal to that of the Supreme Court of Canada. I have my views on the matter; perhaps I may state them in a few words. It is the essential factor of an election that there should be candidates. Without candidates there can be no election. It necessarily follows that votes registered at a time or in a county when or where there is no candidate have no legal value, are worth no more than blank pieces of paper. That is my opinion, but I am willing to abide by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada..
The first principle of responsible Government is the right to vote for a particular candidate and for the man. That rule has never been departed from in any country under the British flag. It was departed from to a certain extent for the first time at the last election, but even then it was provided that the electors could vote for the man. But in the Yukon case the voters did not have that right until after December 31, 1917; therefore all votes cast before that date are contrary to law and contrary to the rights of the parties. But I repeat that I am willing to leave the decision of this [DOT]matter to judicial authority.
As to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada to deal with a case of this kind, I do not think that there is any difficulty. Even the Minister of the Interior

(Hon. Arthur Meighen) and the gentleman who wrote the letter that he quoted this morning, have said that Parliament could pass a law conferring such jurisdiction on the Supreme Court. He could not say otherwise, because section 43 of the Supreme Court Act says:
Notwithstanding anything in this Act contain-*ed the court shall also have jurisdiction as provided in any other Act conferring jurisdiction.
It would be very easy to pass an Act to confer such jurisdiction on the court, but I submit that that is not necessary. Section 60 of the Act provides that the Governor in Council may refer the decision of a question of law to the Supreme Court. It says:
* Important questions of law or fact touching the constitutionality or interpretation of any (Dominion or Pirovincial legislation may be referred by the Governor in Council to the (Supreme court for hearing and consideration.
Surely the present case, which touches the interpretation of a Dominion statute, could, under this provision, be referred by the Governor in Council to the Supreme Court of Canada. I am surprised that instead of passing the Order in Council of February 26 referring this matter to Parliament the Government did not adopt the simpler method of dealing with it by referring it to the Supreme Court of Canada. Let no hon. gentleman tell me that the Governor in Council only can do that. Surely Parliament is superior to the Governor in Council. If an Order in Council is necessary to the marking of such a reference, surely this House may instruct or even order the issuing of such an order. The executive power is the servant, not the master, of the legislative power. However objectionable the assertion may be to their pride, ministers of the Crown are the servants, not the masters of Parliament. Surely a decision of this House confirming the decision of the Committee on Privileges and Elections is equivalent to an instruction to the Governor in Council to refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada, which they have the power to do under the Supreme Court Act.
The decision of the Supreme Court in this matter would be easy of execution. They would either instruct the returning officer to count or not to count the challenged votes, or instruct the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to declare Dr. Thompson or Mir. Congdon duly elected. Shorn ' of all legal technicalities, the question is, can the votes which were given and registered previous to the nomination of candidates-in other words, when there 
were no candidates-be counted under the law of the country as it is to-day? I respectfully submit that the matter of deciding this question does not pertain to the members of the Committee on Privileges and Elections, or to the members of this House. I strongly urge members of the House not to take a step backwards, but to act according to constitutional usage and ahthority and to leave the decision of such an important question to the judiciary of the land.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) attaches a meaning to the report of the Committee on Privileges and Elections and to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin), which it is rather difficult to follow. Both the report and the amendtaent, if adopted by this House, would be admittedly ineffective so far as the two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario are concerned, and, unless the Governor in Council should act according to my hon. friend's suggestion-I will deal with that a little later- they would be equally ineffective so far as the Supreme Court of Canada is concerned. Does my hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) suggest that the Governor in 'Council, or this House, has without special legislation, power to refer this matter to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario. The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Vic-1 toria (Mr. McKenzie) who moved the resolution in the iCommittee admitted that, according to his view, the Committee on Privileges and Elections and not the Governor in Council should have prepared the stated case. Hon. gentlemen who have dealt with this matter do not seem quite to understand what it is they do suggest. Let us, in the first place recall the fact that this matter came into this House by reason of a special return which did not declare any candidate elected for the Yukon territory. Having come into this House on the report of the General Returning Officer, it was referred by unanimous consent, as the House deemed proper to refer it, to the 'Committee on Privileges and Elections. I repeat that, according to my conception, the Committee on Privileges and Elections have made to this House a report which is both impracticable and ineffective, and for that reason I think it ought to be referred back in order that they may make a report such as the House contemplated when the reference was made in the first instance. The question came into this House upon a special return.

The House had the light to deal with that return. The Committee on Privileges and Elections, to whom the matter was referred, had the right to deal with it, and that Committee have left the matter just about where it was in the first instance, I have already said that no hon. gentleman in this House would for one moment contend that this report or the amendment could be carried out in its literal terms. Both the report and the amendment suggest that this matter may be left to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario. Those who vote for this amendment vote tneir belief that this House can properly refer the matter to two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, or that the Governor in Council could do so. The matter would degenerate into a farce if the Governor in Council attempted to do anything of the kind, because everyone in this House knows perfectly well that the Governor in Council has no .such power. So far as the Supreme 'Court of Canada is concerned, neither the report nor the amendment suggests that the Governor in Council should take any action.
The purport of the motion in committee of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) was that a committee of this House should refer the question to the Supreme Court of Canada. Neither this. House nor the Committee on Privileges and Elections has any such power without special legislation. So- far as the Governor in Council is concerned, I do not concur in the view expressed by the hon. member for Kamouraeka (Mr. E. Lapointe) that this is in contemplation of section 60 of the Supreme Court Act. On the contrary, I am impressed with the view taken 'by the Deputy Minister of Justice. It seems to me it was not the intention of that Act to refer controverted election matters.-'because this practically amounts to that-to refer questions Ibetweeni parties, although these matters concern this House as well-to the Supreme "Court of Canada for determination under section 60 of the Supreme Court Act. No. such jurisdiction has ever been exercised by the Governor in Council in such matters in the past, and I venture to believe it was not the intention of the Act that they should be so referred.
Just one or two words more. My hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) speaks of any action toy this House or by a committee of this House, which would not be based upon an exact and literal interpretation of the Military Voters' Act or the War-lime Elections Act, as quite immoral.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I never .said that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend understand that any member of this House during the past session, when those Acts were passed, had it in contemplation that, by reason of such conditions as he has alluded to, three or four hundred men-I forget how many-who have gone overseas to fight for this country and who, equally with the other 300,000 had the right to vote, should be deprived of their franchise? That,
I think, is a pretty important question to take into consideration. This House has rights; the people of this country have rights, and the men who, under the terms of that Act, according to its true intention, were to have the right to vote, must also be taken into consideration when this matter comes to foe determined, and the matter could not Ibe put more clearly than it was put before the Committee on Privileges and Elections by Mr. Congdon, one of the candidates at the recent election in the Yukon. This is what Mr. Congdon said on the 7th of this month before that committee:
There cannot be any doubt that even under the Controverted Elections Act of Canada the [DOT]House of Commons still has jurisdiction over election matters of this kind; that was evidenced by the fact that even in the case of an election petition before a court established under the Controverted Elections Act. the court might report to Parliament, which enables Parliament to go further than any decision which could possibly be given by the court and to come to a conclusion such as the court could not possibly arrive at. The commonwealth is interested in the service of every member of [DOT]the Commons' House of Parliament, and the court and the council of State and Justice of [DOT]which this Committee is the representative is governed by rules of state and law peculiar and more high and more politic than those which govern the court in cases of any matter between party and party. For this reason it ' has always been the practice in regard to matters of this kind not to be scared away by technicalities, not to be hampered by rules which might be binding in courts of Justice, hut to go straight to the heart of the matter, and determine what is just in regard to the matter in dispute.
I do not think the matter could be put in more cogent terms. I may he permitted to recall the attention of the hon. member for Kamouraska to the fact that the Act in question deliberately sanctioned the vote by men overseas, not for a particular candidate, hut for one party or the other in this House. That was the purpose of this Act. Men were authorized to vote either for the Government or the Opposition; and for the very reason that it might, in some instances, be impossible for those men to know who was the particular candidate sup-

porting the Government or the particular candidate supporting the Opposition, that provision was inserted in the Bill presented to the House. For that reason, Parliament sanctioned that principle, and even if there be such a technicality as that hon. gentleman relies on, I think that statute, interpreted, according to the language of Mr. Congdon before the Committee on Privileges and Elections, might not necessarily result in the disfranchisement of three or four hundred gallant men from the Yukon who have fought the battles of this country overseas and who have the same right to be heard in the determination of their representative' in this Parliament as any other man in this country or any other soldier overseas. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) has addressed certain observations to. this House with the greater part of which I agree, but I venture to think that the very argument which he put forward constitutes one of the strongest reasons for referring this matter back to the Committee of Privileges and Elections. He says that if it is necessary, for the purpose of doing What is right and just and fair in this matter, let us have special legislation. Well if we are to have special legislation was it not the duty of the Committee on Privileges and Elections to suggest that to us; and to prepare a draft of that necessary legislation and report it to the House? Instead of doing that they have brought in a report which I repeat is in its terms both impracticable and ineffective. The committee in short has not discharged the functions conferred upon it by this Parliament when the special election return was referred to it, and under those circumstances I think it is eminently right and proper that the report should be referred back for further consideration by that committee. If the committee reaches the conclusion that there should be special legislation one way or the other-special legislation to assure to these soldiers the right to the franchises which Parliament undoubtedly intended to confer upon them, or special legislation for the purpose of making it abundantly clear that some court in this country shall have the power to determine this matter-then let the Committee on Privileges and Elections take that matter into consideration, prepare their draft of the proposed legislation, and report it to the House. For the reasons which were urged by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens, if for no other reason, I would think that the report should be referred back. I am content to leave the matter there, pointing out to my hon. friend who has last spoken (Mr. E.

Lapointe) that it never was the intention of this Parliament from first to last to deprive a single man of those 300,000 who are overseas of the right to vote because he did not happen to know who the candidate was. That I repeat never was the intention of Parliament from first to last, and if there is any technicality in the statute by reason of which the postponement of the election in the Yukon will bring about a different result from that which would have been brought about if that particular contingency had been foreseen and provided for in clear terms in the statute, I still think it is the duty of this House to take very carefully into consideration whether or not they are to sanction the disfranchisement of the soldiers who have voted and whose right to vote is now called in question.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation of last session was of such a hasty character that we need not be surprised if it has resulted in a great deal of confusion, one or two instances of which have already come to our attention. The Act was passed without any contemplation of a case such as we have before us to-day; in fact, many of the points which have arisen in the working out of the Act were not foreseen. For instance, the Act provides that a petition to controvert an election must be presented within forty days of the election, together with the return or no return, and so on. The date for the nomination of candidates in the Yukon was the thirty-first day of December, 1917, and as some of the votes were polled overseas, it was not possible to have a full return of the election within forty days of nomination. The same condition applies in practically every riding, and therefore under the law there could be no petition against an election. I might allude to an election in one of the western provinces which my friends wanted to controvert; we thought there was good ground for protest, and wo were satisfied that if the matter was brought before a court the election would be set aside, but we could not bring a protest at all because in framing the new legislation last year regard had not been had to existing legislation. Another contingency was not foreseen. The legislation of last session provided that the election in the Yukon should take place, not at the same time as the general election, but afterwards, and it should have been the duty of Parliament, primarily, the duty of the Government, who had charge of the legislation and introduced it, to provide for the Yukon soldiers' vote being protected. But

their votes were not protected, and the Act was passed with all the blemishes with which we are now familiar. Provision should have been made to secure the soldiers' votes in the Yukon election, but that was not done, and therefore the. soldiers' votes did not apply.
The Prime Minister a moment ago made a strong point of the fact that the soldiers might be disfranchised. That may be, but it will not be the fault of Parliament, but the fault of the law which did not provide for this case. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior said that the soldiers knew whether they voted for the Government or for the Opposition. In the Military Voters Bill of 1915 provision was not made for the mention of any particular candidate on the ballot; the soldier was simply permitted to vote for the Government or for the Opposition. I called the attention of my right hon. friend to that point last year and the section was amended. Primarily, of course, the Government and the Opposition are at issue, but the candidate himself has always an influence on the elector, and we should not abridge the elector's liberty in that respect m the slightest degree. Everybody in this House knows that many and many a time an elector will be influenced to vote for this or that candidate for other than political reasons, and sometimes for political reasons which the elector will not accept generally, but will accept in a particular case. Again, a man may be in favour of the Government or Opposition candidate, but will not support the policy of the Government or of the Opposition. On the other hand, many and many an elector is in sympathy with the Government or Opposition, bu/t not in sympathy with the Government or Opposition candidate. These considerations influence the voters many and many a time. But the Military Voters' Act of 1915 swept all these considerations aside, and limited the soldiers' choice to the Government or Opposition candidate, without mention of his name.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think I can very positively say that my right hon. friend is falling into error when he says that in the Act of 1915 /there was no provision by which a man could vote for a particular candidate. I have not the statute before me, but my recollection is very clear on the point.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My memory may be at fault, but I do not think so. Supposing I am wrong, I come now to a provision which I certainly believe was
not in the Act of 1915. Here is -the ballot which was submitted to the soldier:
The deputy presiding officer shall sign such certificate and deliver the envelope on which it appears, with a ballot paper, to the voter, who may mark the ballot paper in accordance with the directions thereon as1 a vote for the Government, the Opposition, or any Independent candidate or candidates, or Labour candidate or candidates or for any candidate or candidates (if more than one candidate is to be elected) designated by name for whom he desires to vote;
Whether that is in the Act of 1915 or not, it is in the Act of 1917. The voter could vote for the Government; he could vote for the Opposition, for Mr. Congdon, or for Mr. Thompson, but at the time he voted he could vote for neither Mr. Thompson nor Mr. Congdon because neither Mr. Thompson nor Mr. Congdon was a candidate. Therefore, his liberty was abridged. He could not select as between any candidate because there were no candidates in the field. Will my hon. friend tell me that liiuler such circumstances it is fair to Mr. Congdon, or fair to Mr. Thompson, when the voters could vote neither for one nor the other? That is the reason that all the arguments which have been put up by hon. gentlemen opposite fall to the ground. The liberty of the elector was abridged. If it was intended, as it should have been when it was made the general law of the land, that the law should be applied in the Yukon as well as anywhere else, it should have been provided that voters in the Yukon should vote not before there were candidates but after there were candidates. Why was that not done? Somebody blundered perhaps but it was not done and that is the condition we have to-day. Mr. Congdon, who had a majority of the votes of those who alone could vote in the election, made a protest to the returning officer that he should not count the soldiers' votes. He gave as a reason probably in his own mind, if not in writing, that the liberty of the voter had been abridged in that nobody was named as a candidate and the choice was limited simply between the Government and the Opposition. The returning officer did not decide the objection himself. He referred it to the Governor in Council. I do not know what authority the Government had to deal with the matter when they passed the Order in Council. I suppose they derived their authority from section 19 of the Act of last year which reads:
For the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this Part, or supplying any deficiency therein, the Governor General in

Council may make such regulations, not inconsistent therewith, as may be deemed necessary.
I doubt very much if under this section of the Act the Governor in Council could pass an Order in Council which was passed because it was not a regulation. A regulation would have been passed before the election and not after the election. But they did it. In the preamble of that Order in Council I read this:
The Governor in Council is pleased under authority of section 19 of Part IV. of the Dominion Elections Act, and section 6 of the War Measures Act, 1914, to make the following regulations and the same are hereby made and enacted accordingly.
I do not know whether the War Measures Act would give any power to the Governor in Council but this is the Order:
The general returning officer shall, with respect to the elections in said eleotoral districts of the Yukon Territory, and Nelson, make to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery a special return fully disclosing the conditions and showing the result of the polling and' such return shall be put before the House of Commons for its consideration and for such action by it as may be deemed necessary or proper according to the circumstances.
When this return was laid before the House, the House very properly, referred it to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. The committee met, considered the matter and they made the report which is now before us. In it they stated that-in their opinion the matter should be decided by judicial authority. My hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) who made the motion that is now before the House, took exception to this report. I will read it in order to make intelligible that which is to follow. It is recommended:
That a stated case be prepared and submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision.
My hon. friend from West Calgary stated that the committee ha.d not properly discharged its duty. I cannot agree with him and I believe that on reflection he must come to the conclusion that the point that he has now raised is not justified. The reference is in these terms:
Ordered, that the special return of the general returning officer to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada concerning the election of a candidate to serve in the House of Commons for the Yukon Territory be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections with power and authority to consider the same and the several documents therein alluded to and to report their conclusion and determination thereon to this House.

We have .to-day thalt conclusion and determination. The conclusion and determination, ,as stated here, is that a stated case should (be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to any two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, for decision. They did not take it upon themselves to determine the case involved for the very reasons which have 'been given in this discussion already. The committee is composed of the members of this House and the members of this House are actively engaged in politics. We may make the concession that we are partisans. However honestly we may hold to our opinions. I suppose our opinions and our convictions may be said to be biased one way or the other. The judges are supposed to be and ought to be above party consideration. I think we can say in fairness to the bench of Canada that whenever a man goes upon the bench, whatever may have been his political proclivities in the past, from that time on he leaves them behind' him and goes into 'the matters that are placed before him and decides the cases with which he has to deal according to . law and the principles of justice as he understands them. The committee, of which my bon. friend is a member, has decided, after taking the whole question into consideration, that the best way is to refer the case to the judicial authority. Is there ,a man in this House, on one side of the other, who believes that in a matter of this kind there is a better way of disposing of it than by having a judicial determination of it? If anybody is competent to go into (these matters, if anybody has to decide whether the soldiers' vote ought to be taken into consideration, or whether the Tights of parties or candidates ought to be considered is it not the judges of our courts? Is there any man in this House more competent or better qualified to do this than those who are appointed by law bo be the arbiters between . man .and man? There may, perhaps, be some technicality, but I am sure that had I been a member of the committee I would haye endeavoured to have made the report firmer than it is. I would have left no alternative in it. Even suppose the House adopts the principle laid down by the committee, it is not deprived of its power to supplement this report in any manner that it thinks fit in order to give it the proper judicial interpretation and sanction which it must have. The report does not ask that the decision should be final, but it asks that a stated case be prepared for submission to the Supreme Court of Canada, or to

two judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario for decision.
They can give their decision so far as it can be given, and if their opinion is that they have not ithe authority to determine this matter, then the report will come back and Parliament will take, if need be, whatever action may be necessary to supplement the opinion which they have expressed. I call the attention of my hon. friends to the fact that again and again matters have been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in order to have a judicial interpretation of a point at issue, not with the idea that the court should judicially determine those matters themselves and render a decision which would be binding upon all parties, but to permit the court to give their opinion to the Government and to Parliament so that such action as afterwards may be taken, and should be taken, by Parliament, in the interest of all parties concerned, may have the sanction of the law. Sir, I say this to my' hon. friends on the other side of the House: Let us adopt this report, let the case go to the judges, and whatever decision they give, whatever the judicial opinion may be, it is only an opinion, it will not be a final decision binding upon all parties. Then it will be incumbent upon the Parliament of Canada to supplement that opinion in such a manner as to grant justice to whomsoever justice may be due.

If I might venture to do so, I would express sympathy with the hon. gentleman who moved this amendment, by reason of the fact that those who support him .seem* to me to have furnished the most conclusive argument why his amendment should not be adopted. First of all, I think that the right hon. leader of the Opposition in his main argument has furnished us with reasons which should confirm us in the belief that beyond a doubt the action recommended by this Committee should not be taken. What is the principal argument of the right hon. gentleman? It is that because these votes were taken, under the statute, before nominations, and because provision was not made in the statute for that, that therefore all of the soldier ballots must be rejected, and the soldiers must be deprived absolutely of their vote. And why does the right hon. gentleman say that those votes should be rejected? Because the statute as enacted, if held to be applicable and to permit these votes, would abridge the right of the soldier, because it would
deprive him of the privilege of voting for a candidate by name. And what is his remedy for this grievance? It is to wipe out entirely the right otf the soldiers to vote. Let us say that the statute in its operation did) abridge the right of the soldier, but it still left him the right, in common with all others- to vote for the Government, or vote for the Opposition, and the right hon. gentleman -says: Let us remedy that !by taking a course that will infallibly deprive -the soldier even of that abridged right.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says that somebody blundered. He does not dispute that Parliament in passing the Act in question intended the soldier voter in the Yukon to have the right to vote like every other soldier, tout he says that somebody blundered. 1 presume that I might take that suggestion to myself, inasmuch as I had a good deal to do with the drawing of that Act. How does he propose to remedy that? I blundered, .therefore let us punish the soldier -by taking his vote aw-ay from him. I am far from admitting that under a correct or reasonable interpretation of the statute those votes should not toe counted. But what is precisely the advantage that results from this return being referred to this House? It is that the House w;ould not 'be tied down. Mr. Congdon himself congratulated us upon that. This House would not be tied down to a literal interpretation of the statute, and if the committee had come to the conclusion that that literal interpretation precluded the counting of the soldiers' vote, if they came to the conclusion that somebody had blundered, the committee had it in their power to recommend to the House that the blunder be corrected. But the right hon. gentleman does not -want that to be made possible. He wants this matter sent to a tribunal that will be bound by the letter 4 p.m. of the statute, and no matter what the people of Canada, acting through their representatives desired and intended, although it be absolutely clear that they intended that those men should vote, and though it be absolutely clear therefore that in substance those men had a right to vote-ibecause there is an irregularity according to the letter of the statute those votes shall be -wiped out. I must confess that if I had any doubts in my own mind as to w-hat the proper course to toe taken with regard to

this motion and this amendment was after listening to the argument of the right hon. gentleman I would feel that it was absolutely impossible for me to reach any other conclusion than that this question should remain in t'he hands of the legislative authority clothed with power to provide an adequate remedy if a mistake has been made, and that it would be the most futile of remedies to send the matter to a tribunal that will be tied down to the letter of the law; and, if the right hon. gentleman is correct in his contention, with the only result that we will have a decision that somebody blundered, and because of that fact the soldier must lose his vote. If, in the judgment of the House, that is the important matter to have decided, I tnink we should vote for the amendment. But if, in the opinion of the House, the proper thing to have decided is whether or not men who had a right to vote-men who, by the admission of the right hon. gentleman, failed to obtain their votes because the statute was not made sufficiently clear -shall be, as regards this election, permanently disfranchised, then we should vote down the amendment. I might point out also that it will be no adequate remedy, to say: You may go back and have another election, because those very men whose rights are in question will, under the statute in such a case, have no votes. So the amendment, if it he carried, assures this one thing: That if the statute is not perfectly clear the soldiers will be disfranchised, and the intention of Parliament will be defeated. The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) says that it is the exclusive privilege of the courts to interpret the statutes. That is quite true if you are dealing with the application of a statute, but is it an unknown thing that when Parliament has discovered that the interpretation attached by the courts to a particular Act of Parliament was not in accord with its intention, that Parliament should legislate to give authoritative interpretation to its own statute? And if ever there was a case, it seems to me, where the exercise of that power on the part of Parliament-if there be need to exercise it -would be justified, it is in this particular case. If there be need for it, and Parliament does not exercise its power to effect a remedy, you irreparably deprive all of these men of the right that Parliament itself, with the people of Canada behind it, intended to give them. I do not think that I need add anything further except to ask, in regard to what the hon. member for Kam-
ouraska said as to the clearness of the right of the Governor in Council to refer this matter to the Supreme Court-assuming he is quite right in that contention, whit is it we will get from the Supreme Court? A decision as to who was- elected? An order is issued to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to make a certain return and to the returning officer to count those votes? There is nothing of the kind in that section. What will it be that will come back to us? It will be advice as to what the law is, that is all. Nobody will be authorized to do anything. Parliament will have to take it up, and we will then have to act. And, in my judgment, if there came back to us the advice that, because of the too narrow words of the statute, because, if you will, some one had blundered these men under the strict letter of the Act were deprived of their votes, there would, in my judgment, be no proper course for Parliament to take, having the power to remedy the evil result of a possibly ambiguous statute than to so legislate as to secure to those men the recognition of the effect of their vote.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I did not have the
pleasure this morning of being here when my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) moved his motion, and when my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) moved his amendment, as I was kept busy before the Private Bills Committee. We should get down to the cold facts of this whole matter. What are they? Last year we passed two Acts, the War-time Elections Act and the Military Voters Act. A mistake has been made in one of the Acts. We forgot to provide for the Yukon Territory, which, under the War-time Elections Act is a deferred election. Whose fault is that? I say, Mr. Chairman, that every member who sat in this House last year must take his responsibility for not having thought the matter over and suggested it, and those who framed1 the Bill must take responsibility for not having properly studied its provisions, and for not having provided for this contingency. As a result we are confronted with the situation to-day that a deferred election has taken place in the Yukon, and that no return has been made declaring one of the candidates elected. But such grave doubt as to the proper course existed in the minds of the ministers that they ordered the returning officer to report the matter to the House of Commons. I will read section 3 of the Order in Council of the 26th of February:

The General Returning Officer shall, with respect to the elections in said electoral districts of the Yukon Territory, and Nelson, make to the Clerk of the Crown In Chancery a special return fully disclosing the conditions and showing the result of the polling and such return shall he put before the House of Commons for its consideration and for such action by it as may be deemed necessary or proper according to the circumstances.	_
The special return of the General Returning Officer came to the House and the House decided to refer the special return to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. I should here interpret the genealogy of the events. I ask myself, Mr. Chairman, was this return referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections with a mandate to declare one or the other of the candidates elected and more especially, one of them? No. It was referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for the purpose of inquiring into it and making a report to this House of its conclusion and determination. A majority of the committee has made a report. - Apparently that report did not satisfy the members of the Cabinet and some of the supporters of the Government, and therefore they tell the committee:	"You do not know your business,
we will tell you what to do, and when you have learned what to do, come back and make us a proper report." I am not willing as a member of the committee to accept that kind of teaching, even from the Prime Minister. I have sat in the committee, and have faithfully and honestly considered the case, and I am going to submit what conclusion I have come to, and justify my vote in favour of this report.
I listened with interest this morning to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who talked of hair-splitting. I have always awarded him the palm so far as hairsplitting is concerned, and nobody has come into this House to take it away from him. He says: " You cannot put that reference before the Supreme Court; the remedy is to legislate by statute." My hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) says: " Why should we not legislate by statute and also give the court authority?" But the Minister of the Interior immediately contended that we would burden the court with too much work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I never said that.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend s^id in very words: "It will impose new duties upon the court." This is a special case which is the result of our own fault, because we did not legislate properly, and the Supreme Court has only to substitute itself for the general returning officer and to give
an interpretation to the statute. The Minister of Justice has given an interpretation of the statute, not like the Prime Minister, who says, that if that statute is submitted to the Supreme Court, by the very wording of the statute you will deprive a certain number of soldiers of their votes. I do not consider that we are here to be charged, if we do not admit that the statute should be interpreted as read, as willing to do anything against the soldiers. And under the circumstance of this election taking place after the others, it may well be likened to a by-election. My friends on the other side, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister especially, tried to evade the question by saying: "Are you going to deprive those poor boys of their vote?" We do not want to deprive the poor boys of their vote. We worked steadily at these Election Acts last year, and the Minister of the Interior will give us credit for staying long enough to help him discuss them and pass them.
I remember that the Prime Minister stated at that time that we could not be too careful; that despite all the precautions we were taking, some soldiers would have to lose their votes. And he was right. We could not presume that every soldier who was in Europe would be able to cast his vote. Therefore, there was at the time of the passing of the Act the anticipation that some of the soldiers would lose their votes, and the protection went so far as to provide, in subsection 5' of section 8 of the Military Voters Act, whereby it is enacted:
(5) In any case where, for any reason, unless the vote of a military elector is immediately taken, it is likely that he may not subsequently be able to vote, the Deputy Presiding Officer may take such vote otherwise than at a formally held poll.
There was a provision in the Act whereby the people voting in the Yukon would have been entitled to vote if the Act had been properly put into effect by following certain restrictions imposed under that subsection. If the soldiers' vote was the essence of all these votes, and if the representation in this House was to be based on the fact that all men at the front should give their vote to the man who was elected to entitle him to have the proper status in this House, I do not see why this Act applies only to a general election. My hon. friends will admit that if to-morrow these candidates were both to die we would be compelled to have a new election, and the soldier would not have a vote at that election. If one of us should disappear from this political scene, we should have to have a new election for the constituency affected. What,

then, becomes of all our protestations, of all the eloquence of the Minister of Justice in his remarks on this subject? In a case like that the Military Voters Act would not apply; we wilfully deprive the soldiers of their votes in by-elections. The Yukon election may be likened to a by-election; because that election was deferred, the requirements of the Act with regard to general elections do not apply.
Something has been said about the alleged difficulty of preparing a stated case. The Committee on Privileges and Elections have decided that the matter should be turned over to six judges of the Supreme Court whose duty it is to read laws and to interpret them. After all, the general returning officer undertook to interpret this law. On page 4 of the special report of the clerk of the Crown in chancery, the general returning officer says:
The day for holding the poll within Canada under Part IV of said Act for the election of a member to represent the Yukon Territory is not specifically denominated by said Act, but I have assumed it to have been the intention of Parliament that in the case of a general election, in which case only does Part IV of said Act at all apply, (see Section 1) polling ought to be, as it could proceed for all electoral districts including the Yukon Territory, on one and the same day.
This is what the general returning officer thinks Parliament intended to convey. You say to the members of the Committee on Privileges and Elections: tell us whether the general returning officer's interpretation of the Act is correct; if you say that it is not correct, we will keep you at work until you say that it is, so that we may declare Dr. Thompson elected. I shall say nothing about the reasons which induced Parliament in 1873 to pass an Act taking these matters away from the jurisdiction of politicians. Dr. Thompson and Mr. Congdon are known to most members of Parliament who have been here for a number of years. Both have sat in Parliament, both are able men and are too well known to need any -eulogy from me. I could not pay either of them itoo high a compliment. In deciding this matter, then, where is the line of division? Just your political feeling; jusj, the political affiliations of these gentlemen in the past. Both are eminently qualified to represent a constituency; both would honour the House of Commons by sitting in it; we do not have to decide as to their abilities or qualifications. I confess that if I saw a hole that would sink the man who was not of my political affiliation, I would naturally and humanly be inclined to look upon that hole as bigger than it really was. The -man

who would not see it that way would have to have an aeroplane or some other means of flying higher than ordinary mortals. If [DOT] the reverse were the case, I should be inclined to see the hole a little smaller, so that the other fellow would not get through. That is human nature; that is the reason why these political issues have been taken away from political tribunals and submitted to a judicial body.
This issue has been stated as a mixture of fact and of law. Somebody said that if we were to have a stated case, both parties would have to be represented at its preparation and the case agreed upon by both. I agree to that. But both parties have already been heard by members of the committee. The Prime Minister has read part of Mr. Congdon's statement before the committee. I wish to read part of Dr. Thompson's statement, made through his solicitor, Mr. Hogg, as follows:
Mr. Hogg.-Mr. Chairman, and Gentlemen of the Committee, perhaps I may make it clearer to the committee, acting for Dr. Thompson, what in my view' is before the committee for consideration. There is no matter of fact before the committee and upon which a vote would need to be taken. The facts are contained entirely in documents before the committee. The matter is a pure question of law and the first point of law to be determined is as to the interpretation of the Military Voters' Act which covers the voting of those persons qualified by the Act, that is the soldiers, within and without Canada, That is a matter for interpretation with respect to that Act as dealing with this question as follows: First, does this Act apply to the Yukon, and second, were the soldiers' votes taken with respect to that constituency at the proper and lawful time, and at the only time laid down by the Military Voters Act?
Further on, Mr. Hogg says:
There is a stated case laid before Parliament as to the interpretation of this statute and as to the legality of Mr. Congdon's nomination paper.
This is Dr. Thompson's view of the whole matter. The special report of the general returning officer was submitted to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, as it could be to the Supreme Court, as a stated case. The committee, after considering the matter, have come to the conclusion that the point should be decided by proper judicial authority. Ilf it is said that the report is defective, that is no reason why i; should not be corrected when the. defect is shown. If the law is defective, that is no reason why Parliament should not have the courage to amend iit. Time and again the Minister of Justice has asked the House to adopt amendments to remove ambiguities in enactments. In the Committee on Privileges and Elections we have

no press gallery; there is a kind of muffler on the proceedings. Committees do not [DOT]draw as much interest or publicity as the House does.' If we have erred; if we have not treated the soldiers properly; if we have made a mistake in not making proper provision in the Military Voters' Act under which the soldiers could vote, let us assume the responsibility like men and enact such legislation as will correct the law. If, on the other hand, there is a doubt as to the interpretation, we should not undertake to make that interpretation.
It has been said that the general returning officer is a good lawyer and a man of [DOT]ability. In that I 'Concur. Nobody will dispute the fact that the Minister of Justice is a good lawyer, that his legal experience has extended over many years, and that he is a man of ability. Here are two conflicting issues. The general returning officer says that he took the Apt to mean that the voting of the soldiers would take place on the same day all through Canada for all elections. If that holds good, there is no reason why the votes polled during the general election in the riding of any ho.n. member here should not be counted if a by-election should occur. Supposing some of us should die to-day, if the interpretation given by the general returning officer holds good that you can vote for a candidate when he is not a candidate, and that the fact that you vote for the Government means that you vote for the candidate endorsed by the Government, the same principle must apply in a by-election. The vote is there; the question is there; the issues are there, and there is no reason and I do not think any good reason can be given why the same principle should not apply. The Act is mandatory. There are three things to be done before you can vote for a candidate. In the first place, there must be a nomination. Nominations in the Yukon took place on the 31st of December. Voting overseas ceased on the 17th of December, and there was no candidate in the Yukon before the 31st of December. Does the House wish to establish the principle that people have the right to vote for a man who has not been nominated? If the votes given for the Government or against the Government are to be applied to one candidate or the other, there is .a jurisdiction pre-requisite. You cannot endorse a man unless he has been nominated, and, therefore, the en-dorsation, if given before nomination, is worthless. Subsection 5 of section 12 of the Military Voters' Act says so in as many words:
A vote for a party shall be counted as a vote for the candidate or candidates who has or have been recognized, in the manner hereinafter .prescribed, as the candidate or candidates representing that party in the electoral district to which the vote has been applied. Some recognition shall be made in the case of the Government party by the Prime Minister, in the case of the Opposition party 'by the leader of the Opposition, and in the case of any Independent or Labour party by the recognized leader of such party. Within five days after the day of nomination the Prime Minister, the leader of the Opposition, and the recognized leader of any Independent or Labour party, shall severally notify the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
The Act is mandatory. If not, those votes cannot be applied. In this case nomination took place on the 31st of December, 1917. On the 5th of January, 1918, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada, by virtue of the subsection which I have just read, published in the Canada Gazette the official recognition of Alfred Thompson by the Government party and of Frederick 'Tennyson Congdon by the Opposition party. If you are going to take the votes that were polled before the 17th of December, you will be completely ignoring the Act. The Act says that you shall endorse the candidates within five days after nomination, and if you have endorsed them within five days after nomination, how are you going to apply those votes which were given while there was not a candidate in the field? Under the circumstances I have not heard any answer which would justify sending back to the committee the whole question which the committee has decided not to consider any further, but to submit to another body. The committee has referred' the matter hack to the House. Why should we, as members of the House, saddle the members of the committee with the responsibility of deciding the matter? If legislation is necessary for a reference, let us have it. We can pass it If the House decides that we should pass legislation and say: In the matter of the Yukon Territory, we shall count the soldiers' votes, although, according to law, we are not entitled to do so by any interpretation of the Statute as it exists, let us pass such legislation; but why refer the matter back to the Committee on Privileges and Elections? If Parliament is supreme, Parliament ought to take the matter in hand and respect the wishes of the committee which are expressed in the resolution saying: We want to refer the matter to the Supreme Court; we do not want to assume the responsibility of deciding it. If Parliament thinks the Supreme .Court



should not be given the matter to decide, let Parliament take the matter in hand themselves and legislate accordingly. I do not think it is fair to treat the committee in the way it is proposed to do. We are all members of this House and we have expressed our views. If what is in the minds of those who wish the matter tO' be referred' back to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, is that, when it is so referred back, a candidate will be elected as a result of that reference, I say: Let us act as a whole; let us take the responsibility of enacting the legislation. It is not fair to saddle this matter on the committee for the committee to pass judgment, to sit as a Court of Appeal and say what decision should be given in regard to the matter, and then, when the decision of the committee comes to the House of Commons, the House will say: The report is concurred in, and that will be the end of it. A full discussion should take place as to what legislation we should enact and as to how the matter should be disposed of. I suggest that, if there is any irregularity in the report, we should correct it. If there are any suggestions to be made, let us make them. The Prime Minister has said that the two judges of Ontario should not be mentioned, in the motion. Let us strike out that part and refer the matter to the Supreme Court. If a case has to be stated, the Governor in Council, who has been willing to take the stated case of the general returning officer, ought not to object to have the stated case prepared, and agreed upon by Mr. Hogg submitted to the Supreme Court. I think the Governor in Council does not think less of the Committee than, of the Supreme Court, and what is good for the Committee ought to be good enough for the Supreme Court to inquire into. As Mr. Hogg has said, the question is-shall those military votes be counted or not, and under the Act as it now stands, can we, by any method of interpretation-I do not care how elastic it is-say that the Military Voters' Act goes as' far as to say that votes polled (before a candidate was in the field should be counted for a candidate who later on comes into the field for election? This ought to be looked upon as a by-election as it did not come on at the time of the general election. The general election meant all elections that took place qn the same day and the nominations for which took place on the same day. At the time we passed the War-time Elections Act, we made an exception for the Yukon; we forgot it, and I submit that it is up to Parliament, if we come to the conclusion that 
we are to do justice to the soldiers, to legislate to repair that injustice, but we should not saddle the committee with the interpretation of that law and then put the responsibility on it when the report of the committee is concurred in by this House.

The same opinion has been expressed by the Privy Council in England. Here is a case where the Supreme Court judges would say: "This matter does not come to us under authority from the Governor in Council." Because, if this amendment passes, we cannot compel the Governor in Council to pass it on; the Cabinet is a body of men of independent judgment, and we cannot force them to do it, and, therefore, the case would inevitably go to the Supreme Court direct from Parliament, and, as I said before, the judges would return it, respectfully saying they could not deal with the case. Why, therefore, should we take such a futile proceeding? No matter what the Supreme Court does, no matter what kind of a stated case is made on which to get their opinion, the case is bound to come back to this Parliament. There is no power under the statute enabling the Supreme Court judges to say that So-and-so is elected in such a case as this. All the court can do is to find on facts, and give their opinions thereon. Why should we postpone this case and keep these two gentlemen, who I believe are now in the gallery of this Chamber, in suspense for a year or more, if the case is appealed, instead of taking it up ourselves and deciding at this session what is the just thing to do, not only as between these two gentlemen, but as regards the men who voted ?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the very few words that I shall address to this House on this question, I need scarcely tell you or the House that I do not speak as a lawyer. Edmund Burke said somewhere that while legal training increases greatly the intensity of the human intellect, it does not add correspondingly to its breadth. And Edmund Burke, .sir, was a very great man. Leaving on one side the righteousness or the wrongness of Burke's opinion, I do think, Sir, that this discussion has fallen perhaps too much into the hands of the legal profession and I approach it purely as a layman. And it seems to me to' he one of those questions that can he settled by the rough common-sense of Parliament, or its committees, better than the superfine distinctions of the legal mind. The distinguished layman from Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding)' who spoke on the question for once in a way became more legal than the lawyers, if such criticism will :be considered by him fair and courteous. He referred at some length and learnedly to precedents. Well, that is just what the judges would do. They would settle this thing along the lines of precedents. Why, Sir, all precedents were thrown to the windis in the last election.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONSIDERATION OP THE REPORT PROM THE COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
And my friends opposite say, "Hear, hear." The most striking precedent in regard to the election was thrown to the winds by my right hon. friend opposite (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when he extended the life of Parliament. The election was a year late in being held. My right hon. friend agreed to throw precedents to the winds in an oration as noble, persuasive and eloquent as was ever addressed to this or any other Parliament. Precedents were thrown to the winds because we are in the midst of an unprecedented war.
What was important in the last election was that the mind of Canada should go forth with no uncertain sound' that the Kaiser and the Allies and the whole civilized world should know that on the part of this proud young country there was going to be no faltering until we carried this war to victory. Speaking as a layman, and looking at this question as a layman what is the one question that I have to settle? What the judges would settle the lawyers have not told us; they have a shrewd suspicion, I am quite sure of that. They know how the judges would go about the consideration of
the question. Why they would call up all the precedents of John Mitchell and O'Donovan Rossa and the others we have heard of from the other side of the House. They would look into the musty documents of the past and give an exact technical decision as to the legality or otherwise of the election. What I am perfectly sure the majority of the people of this country want to know about the election is this: What set of opinions will represent the mind of the majority of the electors of the Yukon Territory as they voted in the election, whether in the Yukon or overseas? That is the one question which appeals to my mind. And I agree very much with the remarks that fell from my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) that the opinion of one soldier in this election is of as much importance as the right of either Mr. Cong-don or Mr. Thompson to sit in this House. That is the one question that would appeal to me as a layman, and that is the one question I think that would appeal to the great majority of the people of this country.
With regard to the gentlemen concerned,
I endorse every word that fell from my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) about the House being fortunate if the Yukon was represented by either of the candidates in the last election. With regard to Mr. Oongdon especially,
I have enjoyed his intimate personal friendship for many years, so that my opinion on this subject is most dispassionate. I have always admired his wide culture, his great reading, and his fair and well-balanced mind. If I had anything to say against Mr. Oongdon, however, I should say that in the last election his political affiliations were, to say the least,^ elastic, flexible and adaptable. I do not think anybody who knew how Mr. Oongdon conducted that election could be quite clear that he was a supporter of Union Government. I think there was grave room for doubt on that subject. On the other side, you have an undoubted1 supporter of Union in the case of Dr. Thompson; there is no doubt about where he stood in the matter. The majority of the votes of the Yukon and the imen overseas were cast for Union, and Dr. Thompson was the Union candidate. That is the consideration which I believe will sway the minds of the people; it will certainly sway mine-were the votes for Union or against it, and which of the candidates was for Union and which against it?

So far, so good. But I have far more regard for what was in the minds of the candidates than I have *for the endorsation of leaders. That is how we decide whether a man was for or against Union.
Stripped of all legal trimmings and the refinements of the law, what have we in this amendment which has 'been submitted by the member for Wright (Mr. Devlin)? It is a mere move in the party game. I was charmed with the sentiments expressed by the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) just before he took his seat. Apparently there is no partisanship in Dorchester. Let us rise to view this thing above the lines of party. This amendment is an attempt to take advantage of an oversight in an Act of Parliament to gain a supporter, or a semi-supporter, if you will have it so, 'by the disfranchisement of the soldiers from the Yukon who voted overseas. If I talked all night I could not say anything better than I have just said, and viewing it in that light I shall vote against the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a layman I wish to answer the layman who has just sat down (Mr. Michael Clark). I shall not go into the legal aspect of this question. The member for Red Deer says that the question is: How would the -soldiers have voted? As a matter of fact, how would the soldiers have voted had they known who the candidates were and what they represented? If I were a soldier at the front and had been asked to vote for either Mr. Congdon ot Dr. Thompson, certainly, if I were a Liberal-Unionist-or a pretended one, like the member for Red Deer-I should have voted for Mr. Congdon, on the principle of Liberalism and on the principle of Unionism. The boys at the front did not cast an intelligent vote when they were voting on a ballot the first blank space of which was prepared for the name of the candidate, not for the Government, not for the Opposition, not for an independent or labour candidate. They could not have the name of the candidate if there was no candidate; so how were the boys to vote? The probability is that the majority 
of the votes would have gone to Mr. Congdon, because the bulk of the men at the front are Liberals. Most of the Canadians fighting to-day on the fields of France and Flanders are Liberals, fighting for Liberal principles. What is Liberalism? It is anti-Germanism. Gentlemen on the other side of the House do not seem to recognize that they are the representatives in Canada of Prussian polity and Prussian principle.
The proper thing to do in this case is'to refer the matter to the judicial tribunals of the country. All questions as to the validity of elections have been referred to the judicial authority. In this case, owing to the peculiarity of the vote and of the election, it was impossible for either of these gentlemen to lodge a protest. If one of them had been declared elected, the other could have filed an election petition; but in this case neither was declared elected. The Government stopped the returning officer from declaring one of these men elected, and thus preventing the other from entering the courts; consequently it is proper that this House should give back to that man what they took away from him illegally by Order in Council.

Mr. Speaker, I have an amendment to move to the motion as it now stands. I have felt throughout this debate, to which I have listened very attentively, that a considerable number of hon. members, including myself, are not satisfied with either the main motion or the amendment moved by the hon. member for Wright. Some of us have voted for the amendment and some have voted against it, including myself.
It seems to me there is a sort of middle course to pursue, a course which, if I understood him correctly, is in accord with the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister. This is a large qu^stkn, and in my humble opinion it will not be settled by adopting either the motion or the amendment. The question which we want to determine is the procedure to be followed not only in the present' instance but when cases of this kind occur in the future, andi we make no progress in that direction by voting for either the motion or the amendment.	If
the matter is referred back, the committee have carte blanche to do what they like, and if they decide who shall represent the Yukon constituency we shall still be in the dark as to the procedure that should be followed in similar cases. Like my hon. friend from Red- Deer (Mr. Clark) I would sweep to one side ail technicalities and meet tfce isme fairly and squarely. There is no one on either side

of the House, I believe, who does not want to do full justice to the soldiers and their votes. There is no question here of distinguishing between justice to the soldiers and justice to the candidates, because if justice is done to the candidates, justice is done to the soldiers, and vice versa. If one candidate gets soldiers' votes that he is not entitled to, he is not getting justice nor are the soldiers. The question is how would the soldiers have voted? The candidates had not been nominated when the soldiers voted, so there was no candidate for whom they could vote personally. I also understand there was no Opposition candidate in the field, because both .candidates favoured conscription and .both were supporting Union Government. If I knew that one of the candidates was not supporting the Government policy I would have nothing-to say at this time, although technically and from a legal standpoint that would not alter the merits of the case. But all the reports I have received are to the effect that both candidates stand on practically the same platform. There was no difference as to policy, but there was doubtless a preference amongst the soldiers as to the man who should be elected to support and carry out that policy. As far as I am concerned I might, .as I do, stand for Union Government and the Union Government policy for conscription, but the candidate opposing me might also be doing the same thing, and soldiers would undoubtedly prefer one of us to the other to carry out their policy. The question is now as to the disposal of these soldiers' votes, and whether they can be allotted as the soldiers intended that they should be, or whether they should rightfully not be counted, as was the case in many other instances. If a reason were wanted as to why this should be decided by a judicial body instead of by a committee of the House, I think we have been furnished with a very clear reason this afternoon, in the debate on the question. I do not think any hon. member will say that this House or a committee of this House would approach the case from an absolutely non-partisan standpoint. I therefore think the only thing to do is to submit Tt to the highest court of the Dominion. I do not know just how we can overcome the technicalities in the way, but there certainly ought to be some means of submitting the case to that court. What are those means? I take it from the speeches we have heard from hon. mem-
bers of the Government that there are means of accomplishing this, but that the method is not indicated in the amendment which has just been declared lost. Therefore, without taking up further time as the question has been very fully argued, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) :

The report be referred back to the committee for the purpose of devising means of submitting the matter in dispute to a competent judicial authority in accordance with the long established practice of this House to have controverted elections tried by the courts and not by the House.
