There is no great difference between the condition of the other propositions and this Canadian Northern.
I am sure every member of the House will be satisfied that the Grand Trunk is to he taken over by the country in connection with the Grand Trunk branch lines in the West. I have here a book, Poor's Manual oi Railways, containing' the statistics of all the railways, showing the number of box ears, passenger cars and all classes of rolling stock equipment, and details of earnings, and so on. Anybody with a fondness for statistics on railway matters can consult Poor's Manual, which will be found in the Library. I do not intend to hand out a lot of statistics to the people or to this House, because we have had a tremendous lot of statistics already. We have had statistics on this Canadian Northern until I was not surprised to reach the House the other day and 'be told that they had a surplus of something like $35,000,000. They may have an operating income of that amount, but it is a very remote date till they have $35,000,000 net income. The actual facts are these. The possible deficit on the Canadian Northern for perhaps many years to come, if things were allowed to remain as they are, will amount to about $12,000,000 annually. Everybody can understand that. That was virtually the deficit reported for last year. The deficit on account of the Grand Trunk is something like $9,000,000; I am told it may reach $11,000,000 this year, making a total of $20,000,000 or $21,000,000 of a deficit on these two roads that this country will have to meet by votes every year. How are we going to meet it? We are,going to take these roads over, and we must meet that deficit some way. There is no use arguing that these roads will pay when we are face to face with that deficit. Unless there are betterments tihey can never pay. That is the reason the Government is asked to do something for them. The deficit on the Canadian Northern will be met to the extent of $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 a year by the increase in freight rates recently put in force. About $7,000,000 more will be added to income from that source. About $4,000,000 or $5,000,000, perhaps $6,000,000, will come from the Grand Trunk also from a similar source. That is to say, we have increased the freight rate fifteen per cent, and having increased the freight 
rate we must naturally expect an increase in the income of these roads, with the result that there will be virtually 15 per cent added to their income. Against that there will be an increase, however, in the operating expenses. We cannot expect men to stay loyally with these roads as they have been doing without getting something in the nature of a war bonus to assist them in maintaining their families, and they will hardly be satisfied to receive the same rate of wages as before. Altogether we might expect that one-half of this deficit will be met by the increase in the income from traffic. The Canadian Pacific railway will put up $7,000,000 more, making $17,000,000 out of the $22,000,000; and the Government will have to make up the balance unless something unforeseen arises. Fortunately something has arisen. The railway operations are now controlled by a war board. I made a calculation from the figures given by the Prime Minister yesterday, which led me to the conclusion that if the savings to be made by this board were such as they stated we might expect an additional $10,000,000 or $11,000,000 as a result of the operations of the board, one-half of which would go to the railways owned by the Government. This would mean that we would have about $6,000,000, which would practically wipe out our deficit. If that is done and care is exercised in the management of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk, .there is still hope for these roaids.
We have heard a great deal about the matter of wiping out the investment in these 'companies. The investments in these companies consist of practically three things. First, a funded debt covered by mortgage. Against this there is a fixed charge which we must pay for twenty or thirty years unless we extinguish it in the meantime by a sinking fund-and we cannot do that, 'because in order to establish a sinking fund we should have to continue to buy up the stock out of earnings. Second, guaranteed debentures or stock, third the first, second, or third preference stock. Sometimes these stocks are guaranteed, as in the case of the' Grand Trunk, by floating mortgage constituting a charge on all the valuable property of the road, similar to a second mortgage on a farm or building. These are known as debentures, as distinguished from bonds. Bonds are generally first mortgage charges; debentures are second mortgage, or floating charges funded. When a man gets a railway debenture he knows that he is getting a second mortgage on something, the road,

the equipment, or the net income. The stocks are preference stock; first, second, third, or fourth, with a fixed dividend, and last of all, the common stock. We need not take into consideration the common stock of these roads. The common stock of the Canadian Northern has never paid anything, and, so far as I can see, never will. So that we might as well eliminate that $100,000,000, though we shall always have to carry on our books the $35,000,000 that we pay Mackenzie and Mann for the common stock, and on which	we must consider that	we
are entitled to interest. The common stock of the Grand Trunk paid a small dividend once or twice, but it can also be eliminated by the payment of a very small sum. So that so far as the Can-9 p.m. adian Northern is concerned, the charges narrow down to, first, the mortgage bonds, and, second, the debentures. Most of these bonds are guaranteed. If this matter were placed before arbitrators or judges they would certainly decide that if there were a deficit every year in the operation of the Canadian Northern the provinces should pay their proportion of that deficit, because these mortgage bonds and debentures in certain cases; are guaranteed by the provinces. A fair proportion of the annual deficit on the bonds and debentures that the provinces have guaranteed would be as follows: Ontario has guaranteed some $7,000,000 worth of bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway Corppany. The province's annual payment in Tespect of its proportion of the deficit would, at three or three and one-half per cent, amount to about $210,000 a year. Manitoba has guaranteed $25,500,000 worth of Canadian Northern bonds; its proportion would be about $750,000 a year. Saskatchewan has guaranteed $14,000,000; they would pay about $420,000 a year. Alberta. has guaranteed about $19,000,000; theiT proportion would be about $550,000 a year. British Columbia has guaranteed $40,000,000, and would have to pay about $1,000,000 a year.
The securities of the Canadian Northern are of three kinds, so far as the bonds are concerned: first, bonds guaranteed by the provinces; second, bonds guaranteed by the Dominion; third; bonds and debentures not guaranteed. I have given the amount of bonds guaranteed by the provinces. Bonds to the value of $104,000,000 have been guaranteed by the Dominion, and of unguaranteed seeuritiesi there are $147,000,000 worth. We might eliminate the unguaranteed securities altogether and take over the road if it 133
went into the hands of a receiver, but if has 'been pointed out that that would be a very bad thing to do; and it is only right that we should act fairly to those who have put their money into the road. But there is a very large issue of debenture stock, which is a guaranteed security. Nobody knows who holds that debenture stock, I am told, and nobody knows what was paid for it. An effort should be made by the arbitration now proceeding in Toronto to find out at what discount those debenture stocks were sold, because if we are to undertake to pay for them one hundred cents on the dollar somebody is going to reap a rich harvest. I am satisfied that they did not sell to the public at over 60 or 70. The arbitrators, when they are ascertaining the value of the common stock, should ascertain also the value of that other debenture stock which stands between the common stock and the value of the road. It is a matter of public interest.
I understand that the short-date notes, for which collateral was put in the banks, were under a very heavy discount in New York. I do not think that the railway got more than 75 or 80 cents on the dollar for them. Nobody knows how much was received for them, but they are to be renewed in a few days by the Government, and, of course, the moment the Government goes on those notes they become worth 100 cents on the dollar. Somebody will make a million or two there. These are matters of detail which the Government should take under advisement and which the arbitrators in Toronto should consider in connection with their inquiry into the value of the common stock-what was the actual loss on the sale of debenture stock and shortterm notes?

Construction: completion ot western branch lines already graded; terminals, etc., as per statement, etc.
That means that during the current year the minister expects to spend $7,185,000 on further extending the Canadian Northern. That expenditure may not be remotely removed from the fact that Mackenzie and Mann want to hang on to the road, possibly until the contracts are made for these extensions. I have gone into the question of what these extensions are. The Acting



Minister of Finance should explain very clearly to the committee what extensions it is intended to continue and to complete this year. There is an extension from Calgary to Macleod which absolutely parallels the- Canadian Pacific. The. House should, during the war, frown down on this paralleling of roads. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) yesterday told us we could pull up the rails on the Canadian Northern between Ottawa and Sudbury. I agree with him. There is hardly a pound of traffic between those two points. , He also stated that the rails on that road between Napanee and Toronto could very well be pulled up. Between Napanee and Toronto, the 'Canadian Northern runs within 150 or 200 yards-of the Grand Trunk all the way. If we take over the Grand Trunk, what is the use of maintaining stations along that portion of the Canadian Northern? It will not be the first time in the history of Ontario that roads have been pulled up to obtain efficiency. If you travel along the Canadian Pacific from Smith's Falls to Toronto for forty miles, if you look out of the window on your right hand side, you will see the bed of a road which was built twenty-five or thirty years ago and which was pulled up, everything being removed, but the grading, in order to bring about greater efficiency and economy. It is, therefore, not a new thing to pull up rails and ties on a road. The road between Strathcona and Calgary-that is virtually between Calgary and Edmonton-also parallels the Canadian Pacific. I cannot, for the life of me, see why we should build 32.66 of a railroad there. The proposed 103 miles of railway between Calgary and Macleod will parallel the Canadian Pacific all the way and yet it is mentioned by the Government in the list of roads they intend to build this year. Those extensions are all set forth on pages 1773 and 1774 of Hansard in the report of the speech delivered by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) the other night, and he stated that these proposed lines would cost in the neighbourhood) of $17,000,000. It would be well for us, if we have $17,000,000 to .spend on extending the Canadian Northern, to wait until the war is over, and then after the men come home from the war, looking for work, we can utilise them to good purpose in constructing those extensions. The map shows not only the paralleling system of the Canadian Pacific, but other parallel lines. There are five proposed lines running within a short distance of each other. tained for these, but I think most of the charters have elapsed.

speechtext:
But in the province of Ontario there are places, for instance, in the county of Huron, where the settlers have to haul their produce thirty or forty miles to a railroad. The country that I was speaking about is arid country, only fit for ranching. The hon. member cannot tell me that there are any settlers north of Medicine Hat, until you get near the Red Deer river, along which there are settlements served by the Canadian Pacific Railway line. From the river it goes to Hanna. I do not know if it runs as far as Big valley. That country is largely arid ranching country, and for twenty years before the war w.as given up to sheep ranching. I say without any hesitation that the people of this country should be well advised before they ask any Government to adopt and any Government should be well .advised before adopting the policy of building (branch lines and pioneering when the country is now sweating blood in this war and requires every dollar for the war. I do not think that north of the Red Deer river valley, ,as it is called, theTe are ten settlers. I know the country; it is a ranching country, largely from Hanna south, and for that reason, whatever may he the case in the near future-I grant the hon. member that possibly ten years from now, when all the rest of that country gets filled up fairly well, they will need1 a railroad there. They do not at present need one. If you go through that country, or if you look at the map, you will see that the Grand Trunk Pacific has a road projected running through by Kennersley to Empress and across that same country. I do not wish to be understood as opposed to the West getting branch line railways,
133i
but I say that one-half of the railway mileage built in the last ten years was not required. It was paralleling existing, useless duplicating. What use was there in the Canadian Northern paralleling the Can-dian Pacific Railway from Sudbury to Toronto? It was of no earthly use whatever. There was not enough traffic there to keep one road going. What use was there in paralleling as far as Napanee? What use was there in building a road from Sudbury through the wilderness to Ottawa here? There are no settlers in that country, and the territory was. well served by the old Booth road or the Canadian Pacific railway. I say that without hesitation the same of Ontario as in the West. When the Grand Trunk Pacific was built in the West, if the management of the road had been allowed to build it as they wanted to build it, through the country they wanted to build through, the road would have served a far more useful purpose than it does now. * The original intention was that the Grand Trunk Pacific was to keep fifty or sixty miles away from the other roads, so that it would be a colonizing road and open u.p new territory. But the minute they started [DOT] to build through the West deputations came, down, political pull and pressure was exerted, and the road was compelled to go from one point to another all over the West through what would be known as competitive territory. Now the day has gone by when we need any competition in railways; in fact we have had to raise the rates and put the railways under an operating board., which is convincing evidence to everybody that the day of competition, as far as railway rates and service are concerned, is not now over. The Railway Commission that was constituted fixes the freight rates, and if two roads run into one town it simply means that they will divide the freight between them, and the rate will remain the same. The only other form of competition, and it was the form of competition that nearly destroyed the railroads, was competition in service. At one time three magnificent trains pulled out of Ottawa every night for Toronto within half an hour of each other. Everybody knows that one train would have been sufficient, and in fact the service has been cut down one-half all over the province of Ontario. An effort has been made to prevent duplication of service. The saving will be, $6,000,000 per year. While it is a great hardship to a town to have only one train in and out every day it undoubtedly saves the railways from financial destruction,

and saves the people of 'this country from hearing greater burdens than we are now bearing and must continue to bear for a few years.
When I speak of extensions, I want the minister to understand that we in the East do not intend to vote money for any further extensions into territory in the West already served. I go to the West about twice a year, and not only to one point, but pretty well all over it. I know the various towns and cities growing up out there and the magnificent country areund them. I know it would (be far better for that country if the railways and speculators which own the land all through that country along the right of way were compelled to. give it up and place it at the disposal of settlers, and that would avoid the building of many branch lines forty miles out from the main line to give the farmers access to a market. From Saskatoon westward on the Goose Lake line one-half of the land on each^dde of the road, a6 every member who lives up in that district knows, is not even settled, but is held foT speculative purposes. Would it not be far better if the railways and speculators were compelled to give up that land, which is the best in the West, for the use of settlers? At the present time the settlers have to drive out with an ox team fifty miles away from a railroad to get land, and I have seen lots, of them do that when theTe was rich virgin land lying idle all along the line of railway. Under the present policy the settlers who go out forty or fifty miles from the railway will in time build up a farming settlement, and then some one will come down to Ottawa and demand money to build a branch line out to that settlement, and the branch line to reach that settlement will have to cross these vacant lands owned by the railways and speculators. If the Gov-'ernment are going to take these roads over, they should take very seriously into consideration the question, of also taking over large sections of the farming lands alongside of the roads. When Ontario was first settled we had "string" or narrow farms extending (back along the main road so that there would be enough houses built and families settled along the waggon roads to keep them, in repair. The same policy should have 'been adapted in the West. When the railways wanted extensions they should have released at least a portion of the land along the line, so that the settlers could go in and take them, then the country would have been better served by the different railways as they went through.
[Mr. Currie. 1
I have this to say in connection with competitive extensions, and I think I aim supported by the majority of the members in this House, that this is not the time to expend seven, eight, or ten million dollars in such extensions until we know exactly where we are in out expenditure on the w.ar and on the railways of this country. Within a year or two the railways may be all under one system, and then what use would it (be to have, say, a parallel l-ine from Macleod to Calgary? Nothing of the kind, is desired. Why the Canadian Northern. railway in many cases were not satisfied with paralleling other roads, but if I had time to describe their operations I could show that in several places they have even paralleled themselves or have acquired railways running parallel to their own line and are still running both roads.
Nothing has been said about the finances of the Grand Trunk railway, but I want to say this: You can read Poor's Manual from cover to cover and you will not find a road with as small a funded debt as the Grand Trunk railway, and Poor gives them credit for that. He says their funded debt is almost infinitesimal. I think possibly ten millions would cover the funded debt of the whole Grand Trunk railway with all its branches. The securities against the Grand Trunk railway are guaranteed stock against which there is a floating charge or mortgage, and guaranteed first, second and third debenture stocks. Now you can wipe out a stock, but not a bond security, because a bond security ds a mortgage, and you will always have to pay interest on it until the mortgage is extinguished; but you can always wipe out a stock, unless it is a guaranteed one. So I think the securities of the old Grand Trunk railway, so far as the common stock is concerned, could be wiped out, except $25,000,000; but the preferred stocks, for instance, have received dividends from previous to the time the Grand Trunk railway went into this unfortunate speculation.	[DOT]
The speech of the Prime Minister yesterday was notable. I hope that when a board is formed the ablest men in the country will be appointed to it. If you figure out what the War Board has saved to this country during the last year, since it has been in operation, you will find it has effected a saving of about seven million dollars. I trust the War Board will continue to operate these roads, and that we [DOT]shall only build such extensions as are absolutely necessary. The question is, where are you going to get the steel? None of the big roads are able to get steel

enough, as the hon. member for Algoma said, to replace the rails that are broken and wearing out every day, and broken rails have to be cut up and inserted here and there to patch the roads up. I think altogether seven hundred miles of new road are shown in the minister's abstract. Now what is the use of undertaking this work when we cannot get the rails? The great railways of Canada would buy another one hundred million dollars' worth of rails if they could simply for renewals. They have asked the minister for that, but they cannot get the steel anywhere, because it is required for shells and other munitions. And why should we rob the munitions industry to extend our railways into new country? I say that the service our railroads are giving at the present time is sufficient for our purpose. I know that some members from the West will say: "Colonel Currie is going after the West, and does not want railways built there." If hon. gentlemen will read what I said in the House-

speechtext: May I interrupt? Would the hon. gentleman be willing to stop the building of canals in Ontario and build branch lines in the West?

RENEWAL OR POSTPONEMENT OF PAYMENT OF INDEBTEDNESS.
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: RENEWAL OR POSTPONEMENT OF PAYMENT OF INDEBTEDNESS.
speechtext:
Yes, yes. There is no hope for that railway. I was told in the West, when speaking about the Hudson Bay railway: "It is- a very good thing to talk about if you want to sell town lots." The West has been pretty liberally dealt with and we are quite willing to do the best we can for that part of the country, but there are other parts of the country which are doing their duty just as well as the West. If the building of duplicate branch lines everywhere in the West is -going to be the policy of the new board from now on, I feel satisfied- that this country will be bankrupt inside of ten or fifteen years. The United States did not build its western roads to any extent. They were built by private capital. Outside of the Union Pacific and one or two lesser or greater roads, none of the western roads was built with public money. In Minnesota and through country in the United -States similar to our West, you will not find half of the mileage that you find in our West. The West has tne best system of railways that you can find in any section of the world to-day. The Canadian Northern needs grading much more than it needs branch lines. If it is provided with steel bridges, station houses and terminals it will be able to take care of its branch line extensions itself later, because the Canadian Pacific have shown us that once a road gets upon a paying basis it can build extensions wherever it wants them. For goodness sake, let the people of this country have a breathing spell for a minute or two before you start building parallel lines in any part of the country either West or East. What would be said of a proposal to parallel the roads in -Ontario and Quebec? I do not think Ontario will need any roads for a long time, especially leading to and from the West. There is a part of the riding represented by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) where

there were thousands of settlers-that is Manitoulin Island-and because of the lack of railways at one time many of them had to leave that section of the country, which is fairly fertile, and go where there were roads. Yet, they did not send deputations down here howling for competing branch lines; they took their medicine. There are parts of the province of Quebec where they need colonization roads just as badly as they do in any part of Canada. 1 think I have dealt sufficiently with that feature of the question. Any declaration of an intention to make another grab at the treasury for branch lines until this war is over will be resented by the country.
With reference to the railways, I think I have covered all the ground that is necessary. I wish we had some substantial analysis or an abstract with reference to the Canadian Northern prepared by, say, Price-Waterhouse, or some competent auditors, on the same lines as the other statements that have appeared in Poor's Manual so that we would know how to compare the condition of the Canadian Northern railway with the condition of other roads. We would then know what we were getting. I am satisfied if the proper policy is pursued with reference to this road, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk, the result will be very much more satisfactory to the country. I do not look for anything but deficits for the next five or ten years. If the management is any good, I am satisfied that in ten years these railways will be .self-sustaining and that in twenty-five years they will be able to take care of their own branch lines, their mileage will be materially increased and large portions will he double tracked. They will be a great asset.
This Railway War Board which has taken charge of our railways has inaugurated a policy of switching the traffic. The traffic which arises on the Canadian Pacific is switched to the Transcontinental, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. It would be very easy for that board, if they so desired, with that policy to destroy the premier security of this country-the Canadian Pacific. In that way the Canadian Pacific would be deprived of half its traffic in the West and the traffic routed over these non-paying lines. In this way they can make the other lines pay but they will destroy the Canadian Pacific. I trust that is not the policy that the minister would stand for. The Canadian Pacific has consented and is quite willing to have this tax of $7,000,000 handed over to the other two roads. It 
would have been much easier if an adjustment had been made of the amount of money that should have been collected in rates from these two roads and if a proper war board had been established at the time the war broke out, there never would have been any real deficit from thtee roads at all. But the deficits stare us in the face, and it will be necessary to increase the freight rates payable by the people, and to take one-half of the amount realized from those increased freights and turn it back into the public treasury. .The hob. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) was quite right in his statement that this increase is pretty hard on those who pay these freight rates. If the charges were increased one-half under a war board they would take care of most of the deficits, but the rates have got to be doubled, and' "what the Canadian Pacific makes out of the increased rates is taken away from them by Order in Council and turned into the public treasury. I do not think myself that is just to the Canadian Pacific. Every dollar which that company has made since the war it has invested in far securities, in fadt I think they have put into war bonds over $100,000,000. They are behind the credit of Canada just as much as the greatest public institution in the world. There is no other railroad in the world, for example, that can give you a through bill of lading to. any point on the globe, under peace and ordinary conditions, like the Canadian Pacific. A Canadian who wants to ship goods to any part of the world by the Canadian Pacific railway can go to that company's agent at any station and get a through bill of lading to the uttermost parts of the earth. What is more, if he wants to have his bill collected, he can send it C.O.D. Canadian Pacific to Ceylon or to any part of China, Australasia, or South Africa, and the Canadian Pacific agent at that point will collect his money. Furthermore if he buys goods in any part of the world and wants to check up the weight of those goods or anything else, he will find a Canadian Pacific freight agent there who will do it for him. After the war those agents are going to' be a most potent influence in favour of this country in securing a share of the world's trade. For this reason we should be very careful not to do anything to disarrange the operations of that road. If anybody thinks that a reduction of freight on every road is going to help the country let me say that the Canadian Pacific can carry freight cheaper than any other line and make money on it. All of these other railways

that have been built have beeen loaded up with tremendous fixed charges so that none of them -will be able to carry freight as cheaply as the Canadian Pacific, at any rate not for twenty-five years. Now, Mr. Speaker, the debate over this Bill of my hon. friend 'the Acting Finance Minister has been considerably prolonged, and I regret very much that my remarks haye been at greater length than I intended, but their length was due in large part to interruptions.
Hon, J. D. RF-tD: I do not intend to discuss the merits of the Bill before the committee, but I would like to correct a few statements which have been made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) who has just taken his seat. In the latter part of his remarks, he spoke of the work of the Canadian Railway War Board in Montreal. Let me expand the hon. gentleman's observations on that subject a little and explain the workings of that Board, because I do not believe the people of Sanada realize the good work which it has accomplished. The board was organized in October last, when the heads of the several Canadian railways came to Ottawa for the purpose, and it was agreed that it should operate the several railways of Canada practically as one road. The organization of that board was fully described by the Prime Minister and its record is set out at length in his speech as reported in Hansard. I only wish to say that the Department of Railways and Canals have been working in harmony with the board, and the several Canadian, railways have also displayed a similar spirit of co-operation. Where freight was congested at any terminal one railway has not hesitated in the slightest to hand it over to another in order that there might be the least possible delay. The intention of the War Board is to continue operating the Canadian railways as they have been doing during the last six months so long as the present war continues, and perhaps for some time longer.
It was not with reference to the operations of the War Board, however, that I desired particularly to speak. There is a point that seems to call for a word in fairness to the Government, the people and the Canadian Northern. The Canadian Northern railway has been taken over by the Government ; it is owned by the people of Canada; and it is indispensable for the continued operation of the system that it should be financed by the Dominion Government. I feel that it is hardly doing justice to the Canadian Northern or to the Canadian people that we should continue " knocking" that system from day to day now that it has become the property of the people. It is neoasary for the Finance Minister to go into the open market and raise money to finance the Canadian Northern, and as I said a few days ago, those to whom we apply for the next loan will no doubt have been reading the remarks made by hon. gentlemen in this House, and it certainly will not assist the Finance Minister in raising that money for hon. gentlemen to continue attacking the past history of the Canadian Northern, and giving the public the impression that it does not possess the value, and is not of the good character that it really is. The hon. gentleman makes the statement that the Government, now that it has assumed the ownership of the Canadian Northern railway, is starting out to build branch lines in the West in connection with the system that were never heard of before. That is the' impression I gathered from his remarks, but it is not in accordance with the facts. As I understand the situation, the Canadian Northern, prior to the war, laid out branch lines from certain points along its system in the Northwest. Those branch lines were graded, and in some cases the ties were laid down. Settlers went into those districts and located there, believing that the Canadian Northern, having expended a lot of money and done a certain amount of work, and having promised to build lines, would go on and complete the work. Hon. members have asked whether it is the intention of the Government to carry out the promises, honest promises, that were made by the Canadian Northern in that regard. In view of the promises that were made to settlers that if they would go in along the route of the proposed lines, settle there and cultivate the land, these branch lines would be built, and in view of the large expenditure of money that has already been made on these lines, I do not think it is right for the Government to repudiate the promises that were made to those people that they should get branch lines as soon as they could he constructed.	-

I am going to deal
with that question. So far as the four lines that it is proposed to construct ore concerned, I have gone into the matter thoroughly and there is absolutely no truth in

the statement that they parallel either the Canadian Pacific or any other line.

speechtext: These four lines?

speechtext:
As far as I can remember, I have not the record here. There is an extension of fourteen miles from Gravel-bourg on one line. Between the Canadian Pacific and another road, I do not recall at the moment whether it is the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern, there is a large expanse of country, and the road from Gravelbourg is fourteen miles into a country without railway facilities for many miles on either side of the proposed line. Then there is the Elrose extension. If I remember right-and members from Saskatchewan will correct me-that is an extension to another point where it will connect with the Canadian Northern. If this line goes on it will connect with the Canadian Northern and save a long haul, and in addition will give the farmers of that section the railroad they were promised years ago, and which they would have had if the war had not prevented the Canadian Northern from carrying out its promises. Then there is the Oliver branch, simply extending the present line in that district seme twenty-five or thirty-five miles further on, where the road is already graded and ready for the rails. The statement is made that we are spending $7,000,000 for these few extensions, but that is not in accordance with the facts, because all we are doing is simply laying the rails on the grading already done. And what the Government are suggesting to the Canadian Northern is that the second-hand rails we are taking up on the main line, where we are putting the 85-pound rails, should be put on these branch lines. Then there is another line from Hanna south. I believe the hon. gentleman stated that there were very few settlers in that section of the country. My information from members knowing that country is that there is one of the best settlements of farmers between Hanna and the river to be found in the great Northwest. The mayor of Medicine Hat came down here and assured me that the farmers were in there, and had been in there for some yearsi, that they had this promise, and that if was unfair that these branch lines had not been built. I went into this matter thoroughly, and my information is that if those branch lines are extended millions of bushels of wheat will be raised during this coming season and will be brought out, which never would 
have been done if these lines were not extended.
Another remark of the hon. member w,as with reference to the Hudson Bay railway. We all realize that when that railway was built it was not expected that it would pay for some time. But since the Hudson Bay railway has been built, it is very evident that we must do something with it. Last year it was operated because we were told that there was a quantity of fish which could be brought out, and which was necessary for food' for the western provinces, and also that there were some mines along the railway which could be developed. The result of the operation of trains, which I think ran twice a month, was that the operating expenses were paid with simply the receipts from the fish and the mine traffic.

speechtext: How far was it operated?

You have not carried on any construction work for a couple of years,
I understand? .

Yes, it has not been taken off the contractor's hands. So far

as the province of Ontario' is concerned, I come from that province, and I wish to say that we have all the railways we require at the present time. The hon. member has stated that Ontario has not been building many railways of late, that the great Northwest has been getting them all. If my memory serves me aright, within the last five years we have had a thousand miles of railway built in Ontario by the Canadian Northern between Port Arthur and Ottawa. Then we have had the Canadian Northern built from Toronto to Ottawa, and many other lines have been built in the province of Ontario. So that we have had a great deal of railway construction in this province. I am free tO' admit that a great deal of it should not have been built, there is no doubt about that. I agree with the hon. member that the line from Toronto to Ottawa should not have been built.

speechtext: For part of the way.

speechtext:
Yes, and a great deal of the road from Port Arthur to Ottawa. I only wanted to emphasize the fact, however, that we have had all these railways built in Ontario. Although we have many railways in Ontario, there is a great influence at work in the province to give us more railways, which will parallel each other, too. When the Canadian Northern Bill was up in the Railway Committee a few days ago for extension from Toronto to Niagara Falls, undoubtedly the impression left on the committee was that an electric railway should1 run from Toronto to Niagara Falls instead of the Canadian Northern system. If that railway is built between Toronto and Niagara Falls there is no doubt but that it will parallel two railways that are now in operation. I am not saying that I am in favour of the road between Toronto and Niagara Falls being built by the Canadian Northern system; I am not advocating that at all. But what I do say is that I cannot see at the present time, why there should be another road, electric or otherwise, built by any other corporation from Toronto to Niagara Falls, to parallel the two existing roads. When the hon. member stated that in the West [DOT] the Canadian Northern are now commencing to parallel other lines', I want to say as Minister of Railways-, and on behalf of every member of the Government, that we are not paralleling, and we will not parallel other lines. We will see that the Canadian Pacific railway gets its territory; we do not want to build any railways where they will build them. We will
keep the Canadian Northern away from the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other line; the Government will not parallel any lines. The paralleling of lines is being urged in Ontario toy other railway corporations; that policy has my disapproval in Ontario as it has in the great West. It is the duty of this Government and of the provincial governments to prevent the paralleling of railway lines. That is my policy and I shall carry it out so long as I am a member of this House.

In my judgment, the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) un-

derstands western railway conditions a good deal (better than the member for North Sim-coe ('Mr. Currie). Mention has (been made of the proposed Canadian Northern line between Hanna and Medicine Hat. The section of country from Hanna south to the Bed Deer river is thickly settled; it embraces settlements which are fifty or sixty miles from the Goose Lake branch of the Canadian Northern. This district has no railway facilities. I aim not in a position to say whether south of the Bed Deer river there is sufficient settlement to justify railway construction, tout certainly there is from Hanna south to the Bed Deer river. I am an advocate of the construction of branch lines during the war. The people living in the section of the West from which I come have been patiently waiting until the war is over before they make any demands for the construction of branch lines. Settlers who, even for the last three or four years, have been hauling their products from forty to fifty miles to reach railway communication in the constituency which I represent originally went into those sections of the country because charters had been granted by Parliament to the Canadian Northern and other railway companies to construct lines into those districts, and the people had been promised that those lines would be built. In one section of my constituency the people who have to haul their grain forty or fifty miles to a railway have been there since 1909. The member for North Simcoe mentioned the people on Manitoulin Island1. I happen to have a colony of Manitoulin people in my constituency; they are living in what is probably the oldest homestead district in Southern Alberta. But they have no railway facilities; they haul their grain twenty or thirty miles to the nearest station. These people have been contributing to the development and enrichment of the country, and we shall have to provide branch lines very soon to give them railway communication, or we shall lose them; they will leave Canada and go to some other section of the continent. I went over most of my constituency a few months ago, and in places twenty or thirty miles from a railroad I saw as fine dwellings and farm buildings as you would see in some of the oldest districts in Ontario. That is indicative of the faith which these people have. They are patiently waiting for the construction of branch lines. I have not been pressing the matter on the minister, but the Government would be mistaken in not considering the construction of branch lines 
in the West, because lack of attention to this subject may mean a great lpss to our country through the departure of many of the settlers in the western provinces.
I am satisfied with the position taken by the leader of the Government with regard fo railway policy. I do not believe in 1 the 'Government rushing to a quick decision concerning railway affairs. Proper consideration should be given .to them, and after that consideration has been given it will remain with supporters of the Government and members of the House to decide whether or not the policy adopted by the Government is proper.

The tittle of this House has been taken up by hon. gentlemen on both sides- with

I am going, in a few minutes, to put the minister to the test in order to illustrate to this Committee that even now the Government have not the information to justify it in going on with this legislation. Before I come to that, I want to emphasize this point, that the Canadian Northern railway, unlike every other company or body in this country with which Parliament is called upon to deal, will not supply information. When that attitude is assumed towards me in my ordinary business or private relations, I am willing to accept the challenge, and if I were dealing with the Canadian Northern railway, they would either give the information or get not one farthing of what they were after,-the information would be forthcoming first, and afterwards a decision would be reached as to what they were to -get. I refer to this matter now, because if a stand is not taken upon it by this new Parliament, we shall have the same thing repeated over and over again during the lifetime of this Parliament. I feel I am discharging a necessary public duty in once more drawing the attention of the House to this feature of every transaction with which the Canadian Northern Railway Company and Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are connected.
I agree in the main with my hon. friends on the opposite side of the House who have dealt at length with the provisions, of this Bill and with the 'attitude which the country as a whole should assume towards the Canadian Northern Railway system. I could point out differences of opinion, differences, of view that exist as between them and me, but at the present stage I do not think any good purpose would he served by taking up the time of the Committee in doing that, and so I shall pass on.
I want for a moment or two to refer to the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson), in whose utterances I always take a great interest, but who, like the rest of us, is fallible, and who will not think it unkind of me if I draw his attention to a few slips that he made in the course of his very interesting address. My hon. friend, as was natural in such a general review as that in which he indulged, dealt with the question of railway mileage in this country and the relation which it bore to the population of Canada. I think I am correct in saying that the deduction drawn by my hon. friend from that comparison was that we had too many miles of railway, and that several

railways need not have been constructed. He proceeded to apportion the responsibility, and if my memory again serves me correctly, 'he apportioned the greater part of the responsibility for that state of affairs to the Government previously led by the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I did not happen to be a member of that Government at the time any of its railway policies were determined upon, but I was a member while some of them were being carried out. I do not, however, wish to be understood as disclaiming responsibility for anything for which that Government may fairly be held to be responsible. My hon. friend, in the same connection, spoke of the Drayton-Acworth report, and as he seemed to set great store by that report and to be in general agreement with it, I may be pardoned if I direct his attention to what is stated in it with regard to the mileage of railways in Canada and the proportion which that mileage bears to the population of the Dominion both now and in decennial periods past. At page 10 of the report the members of the committee say:
We may put the same thing in another way. The growth of the mileage has far outstripped' the growth of the population. In 1901. with a a population of 5,3711,3116, Canada had 18,140 miles of railway in operation; roughly, a mile of railway for every 300 inhabitants. In 1911, the papulation had increased '34 Per cent to 7,200,043, while the mileage had1 increased by forty per oent to 25,400 miles; a mile of railway to every 284 inhabitants. Since 1911, the population has, it is understood, not much increased, but the railway mileage open and under construction has grown to 40,584 miles. In other words, Canada has to-day, taking the present population as 7,500,000 only 185 inhabitants to support each mile of railway.
Running over that, for the purpose of giving a summary comparison, it will be observed' that in 1901 the total mileage was 18,401; in 1911, after a period of ten years, it was 25,400, or an increase of 7,260 miles. Starting with the mileage of 25,400 in 1911 the mileage had grown between that year and 1917 to 40,584, or an increase of 15,000 miles-an increase, mark you, which had taken place under the Government of which the present Prime Minister was the leader. I am not advancing this argument, but rather applying it because it has been advanced by the hon. member for Springfield. So that if a mistake has been made in building too many miles of road, if the responsibility is to be placed anywhere, 1 submit that according to the report which was cited by my hon. friend himself the burden of the responsibility must be placed on the sh mlders of the Government of which

my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was the head.

My hon. friend from Springfield also referred to a statement which he attributed to the Government of which my right hon. leader was the head, and which he expressed in these terms:
We were assured by the Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) the railway (the Transcontinental) would only cost the country $13,000,000.
My hon. friend has been out of Parliament for some years, much to the country's loss-and I say that in all sincerity-but had he been in Parliament he would have heard that fable exploded over and over again by hon. gentlemen among whom he is now sitting and by members of the Government of which he is now a follower. The last time I have a distinct recollection of that argument being taken up and refuted was by the hon. Mr. Justice Lennox, the former Conservative member for South Simcoe, I believe, at all events one of the Simcoes; and when I have time I will refer my hon. friend to the page in Hansard containing Mr. Justice Lennox's refutation of that argument.
My hon. friend from Springfield also referred to the investigation which was carried on by the commission appointed by the late Government into the construction of the National Transcontinental railway, a commission known as the Gutelius-Lynch Staunton Commission. My hon. friend asserted, -without referring to the findings of that commission, but using a phrase which has done great service in the headlines of the Conservative press in this country, and which has been worked to death on Can-servative platforms all over the Dominion, -that the finding of that commission was that " there was $40,000,000 of graft money in connection with the construction of the National Transcontinental railway."' Now I wish to give that statement made by my

hon. friend-made in good faith I have no doubt, and without having looked alt the report of the commission-the most emphatic and unqualified denial. No such finding was made by that commission, because no such finding could have been made, and no such report was made by that commission. What did the report of that commission say? It said:
We find that without including money which was unnecessarily expended in building the railway east of the St. Lawrence River, $40,000,000 was needlessly expended in the building of this road.
And then the commissioners go on to say what they mean by "needlessly expended." They say that the permanent work should not have been permanent, but temporary work, that trestles should have been put in instead of fills and bridges, and that the road, instead of being constructed on a four-tenths grade in one direction and a six-tenths in the other, should have had velocity grades; in other words, that the character of the road should have been cheapened,, -and ftha't if this cheapening process had been carried out from start to finish the cost of the road would have been $40,000,000 less. That is the finding of that commission, and not that $40,000,000 of graft was obtained in the construction of the road. I mention these things because from my limited experience in Parliament I find it is a mistake to let such statements go unchallenged. It is an injustice to new members who may not know the facts, and who, if the state-[DOT] merits are left unchallenged, will believe them and give them circulation throughout the country. That is the reason why I have gone to the trouble of quoting chapter and verse for my hon. friend from Springfield, who I know desires to be fair in this as in all other matters of public criticism.
Coming to the Bill itself, I submit that it is open to the same objections as were urged againt two measures introduced into this House a little earlier in the session, one of the them by the Minister of Railways and Canals. I refer to the measure by which he proposed to withdraw from Parliament control over a certain annual expenditure. Hon. gentlemen will recall that opposition to that measure was so marked and so general in this House that the minister wisely withdrew his Bill. I submit that the Bill we are now discussing, Bill No. 87, is open to the very same objections. This Bill, if passed, will deprive Parliament of the control of the expenditure made in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway system, and I am
sure that that has only to be pointed out to hon. members, and particularly to those who have already criticised the Canadian Northern Railway management and who know something of the manner in which the management carry on their transactions, to secure their approval of a proposal that this Bill should be so amended as to make it apply to the- expenditure for one year only; so that the Government and the company will have to come before Parliament each year and submit a statement of what the expenditure has been and is to be and secure approval for that which has been spent and authority for that which is to be expended in the current or the coming year. If we do not do that, if we pass this Bill in its present blanket shape, this Parliament will, with its eyes open, have divested itself of all control of these expenditures. Parliament, I am certain, does not intend to do that. It is quite possible that in the rush of work this session, and owing to the continuous strain upon members, due to the long sittings, that feature of the Bill may not have presented itself to them.
I am trying to draw attention to it now. My submission is that both the first section and the preamble should be entirely re-cast so as to make this Bill apply only to the expenditure of the current fiscal year. speechtext: It appears to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Murphy) who proposed the amendment . must be losing sight of the fact that the Canadian Northern is the property of the people, upon whom all of the outstanding securities of the Canadian Northern are a direct obligation. The Finance Minister will not be renewing obligations for a private railway company when he renews, either this year or next year, any obligations that are outstanding or maturing, chargeable against the Canadian Northern Railway property, and I submit this question: Will the Canadian people or the Parliament of Canada be acting "wisely in tying the hands of the Finance Minister? If the opportunity arises during the present fiscal year of renewing any part of the outstanding obligations of the Canadian Northern Railway system on the basis of an interest charge similar to what they have been carrying for the past ten years, will he be wise in renewing them or will he be not? Let me put it this way: I assume, and I believe that every hon. member in this House will assume, that many of the obligations maturing this year are held by parties who hold obligations that will be maturing next year. Now, if the opportunity is presented to the Finance Minister during the present year of renewing both sets of obligations on the old terms, will he not be wise in availing himself of that privilege? If we tie the hands of the Finance Minister and say to him that he can only renew the obligations that are maturing up to 31st March, 1919, we are placing him in a position that will not make it possible for him to take advantage of the fact that you can without question extend the time of a large block of securities much more readily than you can a small block of securities. If the Minister of Finance can, during the present fiscal year, extend the time on every single dollar of outstanding securities that the Canadian Northern have for a period of ten or fifteen years, he would be doing good business to seize the advantage and do it, because we know these securities were sold at a price and at a rate of interest that could not possibly be obtained if we went into the markets of the world and endeavoured to sell new securities to-day. So that I say that the House will be acting very wisely if it does not tie the hands of the Finance Minister in any degree in extending the time on any part of these securities, if it is possible for him to do it.
