House again in committee on Bill No. 83, to amend the Special War Revenue Act,
1915-the Minister of Finance-Mr. Boiyin in the Chair.
On section 5, 19B, subsection 1-tax on articles in schedule:
Is this tax to be paid when the goods are completed and put into stock, or when they are sold to the retailer?
It is payable when the goods are sold.
Is that clearly stated in the Bill?
The words used are " manufactured and sold ".

Subsection agreed to.
On section 5, 19B, subsection 2-automobiles and jewellery in stock on 30th April liable to tax:

This subsection says':
There shall be levied, collected and paid upon automobiles and jewellery imported into Canada.
I understand, when an automobile is imported into Canada, this duty will be paid.
Yes.
If it is imported for sale?
Yes.

The subsection says for
sale or manufacture. I understand when an automobile is imported into Canada it is generally manufactured. It is all set up except the wheels which are tied on the side. When the automobile is taken out of the car, the only thing to be done is to put the wheels on. Does the word " manufacture " apply to the word " automobiles " or just to the word "jewelry "?

It applies to
both.
If the automobile is imported into Canada, it cannot be for manufacture unless the parts are to be manufactured.

The word "imported " comes first. The word " manufacture " should be "manufactured". I move that the word " manufactured " be



substituted, for the word " manufacture " in line 42 on page 3 of the Bill.
Amendment agreed to.

I have to renew the
objection which I made to the resolution concerning automobiles when the .Acting Minister of Finance brought down hie Budget. I take the liberty of again pointing out to him that the word " automobile " is a very broad term* and could properly be applied to such widely separated vehicles as tractors or heavy trucks and the most expensive and luxurious touring care or limousines. From replies made to me by the minister when I was endeavouring to criticise the Budget speech, I understood that the word "automobile" was practically restricted to pleasure cars. If that be so, it should be so stated in the Bill. The term is so wide that there is bound to be misapprehension and confusion unless it is more closely defined.

Was my hon. friend's attention drawn to the schedule to this Bill? The word "automobile" is there defined:
Automobiles adapted or adaptable for passenger use.
It was intended that the tax should apply only to such classes of automobiles.

I am afraid that definition, although it helps a great deal, does not altogether clear away the difficulty. I am afraid it will suggest to people's minds that automobiles adapted or adaptable for passenger use are automobiles for the carrying of passengers who pay money for that privilege. Let us take Ford cars with an interchangeable rear part which are used as express cars, but which can be used as pleasure cars. Would such cars be exempted?
No. They would not be liable to the tax.
The schedule says: "adapted or adaptable for passenger use."
Passenger automobiles are sometimes used for delivery purposes by the removal of the body from the truck. That class of automobiles would be subject to the tax.

Is it the intention to give people who have a stock of those cars an opportunity to dispose of them before the tax is collected, or has the manufacturer to pay the tax as soon as a car is manufactured? An excise tax is generally payable

only when the article is sold. The article is supposed to be in bond1 until it is sold to the consumer. I was called up by long distance telephone to find out in regard to this matter.
The tax will be paid only when the car is sold.
That is to say, the numbers of the cars that have been imported and stored in the warehouses can be handed in to the department and the tax paid as they are sold to the buyers.
That is, if they were imported before 30th April, and in stock at that time, the tax will be paid only at the time of sale.
Wha't about cars manufactured in Canada?
The tax on cars manufactured in Canada is payable at the time of sale.

The duty on automobiles being now 421 per cent if you add this 10 per cent duty on automobiles that are imported, although you do attempt to equalize that by the exercise tax on automobiles* manufactured in this country, you are practically putting the users of automobiles at the mercy of the automobile manufacturers of this country, because our import tax of 521 per cent on automobiles will absolutely reserve the whole market for the Canadian manufacturers. The 10 per cent excise tax will be altogether inadequate to equalize the situation as between the manufacturer and the importer. The minister should carefully consider whether, in imposing this extra 10 per cent import duty, he should not very substantially increase his excise tax on automobiles manufactured in Canada. If he puts the consumers at the mercy of the Canadian manufacturers, he will get a 10 per cent excise tax, but if he shuts out altogether the importation of automobiles he will lose the 421 per cent he is collecting now on cars brought in, and the last state, so far as the treasury is concerned, will be worse than the first.

As we are putting a tax on automobiles I think the minister should consider the advisability of fixing the price of gasolene of the price prevailing in the United States. Over there they pay twenty-two cents, compared with our thirty and thirty-five cents per gallon. Would it not be advisable to put a tax of five cents* per gallon of gasolene? That would bring the

price of gasolene in Canada up to about thirty cents and the Government would get five cents a gallon in taxes.

I did not give any consideration to the fixing of the price of the gasolene when considering the imposition of this tax, but I may say that the matter of the price of gasolene has received some attention from the Government, and .it is to receive further attention very shortly. I do not think the difference between the price of gasolene in Canada and the United States is .as great as the hon. gentleman suggests. In the first place he must remember that gasolene is sold in the United 'States by a different measure from ours, and that accounts for a difference of three cents per gallon. Then the question of transportation enters very largely into the cost.
If gasolene now comes in free, I cannot quite understand the argument of my hon. friend.

There is no argument in' favour of charging the people of Canada ten cents more for gasolene than the people of Windsor and Detroit are paying. It is true there is w duty on gasolene, but I cannot understand why gasolene can be purchased in the United States at twenty-five cents an imperial gallon at Detroit or Buffalo, and as soon as you cross the river it costs thirty-five cents. This country is not benefited at all by this additional price, and I think it would be advisable for the minister to take into consideration the fixing of a price for gasolene, just as the price is fixed in the United States, making an allowance for the difference between the imperial and the wine measure.
Is the price fixed in the United States?

It is, because you can buy the wine gallon for twenty to twenty-three cents in the remotest parts of the Southern States. At Chicago, Detroit, Buffalo, and all through that territory it sells for from twenty-three to twenty-five cents, but when you cross the river it is thirty-five cents. I think the Government, when putting a tax on automobiles, which are a luxury, should also take into consideration the fixing of a price for gasolene for these automobiles, because gasolene is very much used by the farmers nowadays both on the farm and in trucking. I think the price of gasolene should be fixed so that Canada will not be imposed upon, and a little tax upon gasolene might probably get the Government more revenue than the tax on automobiles.
134J

I do not know where my hon. friend found the price to be twenty-three cents per gallon in the United States and thirty-three cents in Canada. The last time I was over there the bigger gallon sold for thirty cents, a-s compared with thirty-three cents here, and thirty cents there is exactly equal to thirty-six cents here.

I understand that gasolene is cheaper in Toronto at the present time than in Buffalo. It is very difficult to explain the spread in price, tout had I known this question was coming up to-night I would have had some information on the subject which would have helped in the discussion. I may assure my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) that certain representations have been made to the Government in respect to the price of gasolene, and we are proposing to make some inquiries into the matter.

I think the question
raised by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) is very apropos. He wanted to know whether big motor trucks would be subject to this tax.
That has been explained.

Personally, I do not know of a motor truck that cannot be adapted to passenger service. Let me give an illustration. A truck was imported, something like the ones that are seen in the streets of Ottawa sprinkling water. It wore out, and was sold to a couple of fellows who took off the tank and put on seats, and now the car is being used to transport passengers between two villages. That goes to show that any automobile is adaptable to passenger purposes.
It was not in that condition when it was imported.
Who is going to decide if it is adaptable for passengers when it is imported? I say there is no truck that is not adaptable for passengers.

I do not think there will be any serious attempt to evade the tax by importing an automobile as a motor truck, and afterwards converting it into a passenger automobile. I do not anticipate there will be any trouble on the part of the officials of the Customs Department in giving a satisfactory ruling in every instance. You can convert possibly almost any motor vehicle into a passenger car, but I would point out that the cost of a motor truck is very much greater than the cost of a passenger automobile.
Is the tax applicable only to automobiles brought in for sale or for manufacture?

Applicable to
every automobile imported.
The clause reads, "Automobiles imported into Canada for sale or manufacture."
That is in respect of stock on hand on the thirtieth of April, stock already imported.

I should like to make a suggestion with reference to taxing automobiles, and the object of my suggestion is not only to increase the revenue but by taxation to discourage the purchase of luxuries and unremunerative articles. I would suggest that instead of a flat rate of ten per cent on motor cars a sliding scale be adopted, taxing motor cars costing 31,000 or under say ten per cent, cars costing $2,000 twenty per cent, and on the more luxurious cars and limousines costing $3,000 or over, a tax of thirty per cent of the selling price. I think motor cycles should also be included in this scheme of taxation. They cost anywhere from $300 to $500, and, of course, are pleasure vehicles.
I do not see any reason why motor cycles should be excluded. You would derive an increased revenue from this source. The imposition of a tax on the lines as suggested might discourage the investment of money in luxuries. I would endorse the proposition made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that a tax of five cents a gallon should be levied on gasolene when used for pleasure purposes. Gasolene as used for industrial or utility purposes should be exempt, hut when it it used for purely pleasure purposes I do not see any reason why you should not levy a tax on it. In the Old Country they prohibit the use of gasolene entirely for pleasure purposes.

It would be very difficult to administer a tax on gasolene unless it were made applicable to all uses. Gasolene is used very largely by farmers, particularly in the western provinces, and by fishermen on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. The question of the taxation of gasolene received very considerable attention. I do not know that I should state to the House what considerations influenced me in not including such a tax in this Bill. Possibly it may be imposed next year. The price of gasolene is now very high and possibly it may go higher owing to the fact that the cost of crude oil has advanced

between 200 and 300 per cent. Crude oil, from which gasolene is made, sold before the war for 95 cents a barrel. Three weeks ago it was selling for $3.95. It is believed in the United States that it will go a great deal higher.. The supply of crude oil in the United States to-day will not meet their own wants for fuel purposes. It was that consideration which largely influenced the Government in abandoning the idea of a tax upon gasolene for this year at least. The suggestion about grading the tax on automobiles has merit, of course. However, as long as it is based upon the selling value, the more expensive car will pay more than the cheaper one. The larger proportion of automobiles purchased or manufactured in Canada cost under $1,000. In Canada last year there were manufactured 68,000 automobiles which were sold at a price under $1,000. There were 8,000 sold at a price between $1,000 and $2,000, and 400 only over $2,000. The number of imported automobiles costing over $2,000 was very small indeed. It was for that reason that I thought it better to make the tax applicable to all.

I see no definition of the word "jewellery" in the Bill. The only paragraph I can find, having reference to the matter, is that in the schedule to part IV, which says:
Articles commonly or commercially known as jewellery, whether real or imitation, for personal use or for adornment of the person.
Will that include medalb given as rewards in schools, convents, colleges and universities? Many of these medals are manufactured in Montreal, and I have received some inquiries as. to what would be included under the word "jewellery." Will religious medals be included? The paragraph reads in such a way that these medals might be classed as "jewellery," because it says, that the tax shall apply when these articles are acquired for personal, use or for adornment of the person. Some of these imedals are worn because they have been bestowed as a reward or a distinction.
iMr. A. K. 1VLACLEAN: I think I may 6afely say that a. medal will hardly come within, the definition, of the word "jewellery."

The Acting Minister of Finance did not deal with the suggestion to include motor cycles in the articles subject to taxation,. I do not see why they should not be. A motor cycle is as much a pleasure car as any other car, and it should bear taxation as well as the cheaper motor cars.
No, it was nor intended to include them.

I think they are a great nuisance, and) if they were taxed out of existence it would not ibe a bad idea.
Mr. MoMASTER: I do not wish to importune the minister, but it was a serious argument I advanced which he has not replied to', namely, that when he puts the duty as high as 52J per cent he will in a large measure reduce the revenue to be derived from that source. It may possibly be that that is the object-to stop imports from the United States.
That was one of the objects.
If that is so, well and good, but it will not help the revenue.
The minister has not given answer to my question as to whether medals are included within the term "jewellery."

I could not speak definitely about that matter, because the department administering the Act will have to frame regulations as to what will come within the definition oif jewellery from time to time. I am only giving my opinion, which is that medals would not be classified as jewellery. I think the Department of Customs would take the definition of medals that is found in the Customs Act, and exclude them from the tax:
Medals, of gold, silver, or copper and other metallic articles, [DOT] actually bestowed' as trophies or prizes and received and accepted as honorary distinctions, and cups or other metallic prizes won in bona fide competition.

Will this tax apply to watches, including wri6t watches?
(Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: No.
I think the clause should be amended so that it would be demonstrated beyond all doubt that it does not apply to medals.

I do not think
it is an important matter anyway, because the amount taxable would be very small. I think my hon. friend can afford to let the matter drop.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 3-Tax on tea.

This subsection
is indefinite. It refers, as far as I can understand it, to tea that was in warehouses on April 30, and does not cover tea that was purchased after that date.
This is the excise tax. The other is in the Customs Act.

Could not the
minister get along without this tax on tea?
It is very unpopular. Tea is a beverage of the poor man and the poor woman, in fact of everybody. The fact of whisky being prohibited makes it all the harder-
I should think that would make it easier to pay the tea tax.

-harder that this heavy tax should be imposed on the only beverage that is left for the people. I think the minister ought to be able to carry cn without this tax on tea. It is one of the taxes that we have not levied in the past, and it appears to me that he ought to give the matter some further consideration. My view would be that this tax should be struck out.
Mr. PEDtLOW: I quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) in regard to the tax on tea. I think if the minister were to transfer the tax from tea to gasolene he would obtain as much revenue, or more, and would please a lot of people. To change this tax from tea to gasolene might displease some persons, but I am sure the pleasure that the tea-drinkers would derive would more than overcome any displeasure that such a change might cause.

A tax upon anything is unpopular. But, unfortunately, we must have a revenue, and it must be imposed upon things that enter into consumption. The consumption of tea per capita in Canada is about four and a quarter pounds per year, so that after all the tax will not be a very onerous one. I would be very pleased indeed if we did not have to impose it, but I think the people of Canada will accept it in good spirit.

I can quite understand that it is as impossible to tax and be popular as to love and be wise, but when when we are taxing tea let us proceed in accordance with proper principles. I am urging once more-and it is only proper that I should do so-that this excise tax on tea should be ad valorem and not a specific tax. You are taxing at ten cents a pound the thirty-cent tea used by the poor, which means an imposition of 334 per cent, while the tea costing fifty or sixty cents a pound, used by the richer people, is only taxed to the extent of fifteen or twenty per cent. This is not a fair

or a right way to impose taxation. In the second place, I see no reason for departing from the principle introduced in 1897 of a British preference. A British preference should he granted to the tea growers of Ceylon and other parts of the world where the British flag flies. I see no reason for departing from that policy, and I would urge upon the minister even at this eleventh hour to change his tax to an ad valorem one, and to preserve the British preference in regard to tea.

I think it is absolutely impossible to have an ad valorem tax on tea. In the first place, it would be very difficult to administer such a tax, and in the second place it would yield very little revenue. If you have an ad valorem tax upon tea importations it must be upon the price in the country of production. In India, China, and Ceylon, tea sells at four, five and six cents a pound. It would not be fair to the British exporters of tea to this country. Then I am informed by the officers of the department that almost all the countries of the world regard an ad valorem tax upon tea as being practically impossible. The only countries which have an ad valorem tax are Turkey, China and Egypt. At the present moment the British tax upon tea is a shilling a pound; in France, I think, it is twenty-four cents a pound, and in Italy it is even higher. I think I may safely say that an ad valorem tax on tea would yield very little revenue, and it would practically be impossible of administration. Now, as to a preference to importations from British countries, I repeat what I said a few days ago, that the suggestion is worthy of consideration. At the present moment we are in need of the revenue and we thought it advisable to put this tax in the same category as the tax upon tobaccos and liquors; in regard to which a preference is not given to any of the British countries. However, the matter may receive the consideration of the Government later. I want to point out also that for the present year a preferential rate for the British dominions would not carry any advantage owing to the impossibility of getting shipping to forward tea. The suggestion of my ihon. friend, however, is a very fair one, and I quite agree with him that it is worthy of consideration.

Does not the minister
think that the tax should be 20 per cent ad valorem? The man who buys tea for 25 
cents or 50 cents a pound would then pay 5 and 10 cents. And if he bought tea for $1 a pound, he would pay 20 cents. The minister has referred- to the consumption of tea in France. Tea is not drunk in France, not because it not used, but because coffee is drunk to a greater extent, and the drink of the poor man is not tea, but coffee. So the poor man ie not hit as hard by that tax in France as we are here.	[DOT]
Tea is the great article in Great Britain, not coffee, and I think Canada is- a tea-consuming country.

Absolutely. Tea ie the
poor man s drink in Canada. Xf we made the tax 20 per cent ad valorem, the tax on fifty-cent tea would be 10 cents and on dollar-tea 20 cents.
Is there any dollar-tea?
Yes. I think I have paid as much as $1.50 for tea.

There is no such thing as importations of tea costing 50 cents. The export prices now from British India are 7.27 cents per pound; Ceylon, 6.56 cents; China, 5-1 cents; Japan 7.10 cents. 'The export prices are just as I have given, and the 50 cent tea sold in Canada is blended by Canadian tea houses.. Of course, blended tea also comes from Great Britain!

Does the section provide that this tax shall only apply to dealers holding 1,000 pounds of tea- at a time? In a great many cases, especially in the big towns, there are many small dealers holding only a few hundred pounds of tea.
They do not pay.

But they are charging ten cents to the consumer just th^ same. The consumer is paying at this time of the year in Ottawa 10 cents excise tax which the corner-store dealer pockets. When the departmental inspector goes to the dealer, he will prove that he has not a stock of
1,000	pounds of tea, nevertheless he is charging 10 cents to the consumer just the same. Why is the provision limited to a minimum stock of 1,000 pounds? There is no way of the consumer getting back his money, and' the dealer will usually be sharp enough to get the ten cents. If the consumer is paying the tax, the Government should take means to get it, and not allow the dealer to pocket it. -

I do not think it is correct that in all places the dealer has

added already the tax to the price of stocks now on hand. If stooke of tea on hand regardless of quantity had to pay the tax, it would cost more to collect the same than we should receive. It might be possible to have collected the tax upon aH stocks on hand in the large cities. But if the Department of 'Customs and Excise were obliged to send their officers all over Canada, through the country districts collecting ten cents a pound on every pound of tea held by merchants, my hon. friend will readily see that that would be a very expensive operation, the net result of which would be that the treasury would be out of pocket. We had to fix a limit and we thought
1,000	pounds about right.
I understand that. But in order to collect the tax at all, your collectors will have to visit every store, to find out what amount of tea is on hand.
Now they do, but hereafter the tax will be paid through the customs.
What amount does the minister expect to get from this tax on tea?
As many hon. members have said, a heavy tax is being put on tea. But I think coffee should not be neglected.

Oh, we have not forgotten coffee.
On section sub-paragraph (4)-Tax on moving picture films:

I would suggest that
a different basis would be, perhaps fairer on taxes of this kind and not decrease the revenue in any way. Instead of a flat rate of 10 cents, or whatever the rate is, _ a graduated rate on films and moving picture theatre tickets and other theatre tickets might be imposed. For instance, it is hardly fair that expensive tickets costing $1.50 and $2 should only pay a minimum tax of 10 cents each. I think any one who is flush enough to spend $1.50 or $2 on a theatre ticket can well afford to pay 25 or 50 cents in addition. I think that feature should be looked into if it has not been already.

If the war continues very much longer there will be ample time to create further additional taxes, if up to the present time we have overlooked any. Theatre tickets are now
taxed by all the provinces. In some places there is a municipartax as well. I think it is better that we do not enter into conflict with the provinces and municipalities in matters of this kind, at least so long as we can avoid it.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean the House .adjourned at 11.59 p.m.
Friday], May 17, 1918.
